articles.title: ‘It all happened in a split-second’: survivors recount details of Spain’s second deadly train crash in 10 months
articles.summary:
Passengers describe carriages full of seriously injured people after crash that has claimed at least 68 lives

Josimar Medina woke a little before 9am on Wednesday to find himself airborne…

blocks.text: Josimar Medina woke a little before 9am on Wednesday to find himself airborne and hurtling through his carriage on the fast train from Madrid to Seville.
“I remember flying through the air and looking for my girlfriend, who was also shooting through the air,” said Medina, a 37-year-old tourist from the northern Peruvian city of Chiclayo.
Once he landed, he looked around and realised just how lucky he and his girlfriend, Vitoria Maia, had been.

“I saw people with cuts, people covered in blood, people missing limbs, and I saw one person who had nothing left below the chest,” said Medina. “I saw people with their heads crushed and people with mutilated arms.”

blocks.caption: Josimar Medina and his girlfriend Vitoria Maia, from Peru and Brazil respectively, were thrown across their carriage of the fast train from Madrid to Seville after it collided with another train on the track. Photograph: Sam Jones/The Guardian

blocks.text: The Peruvian stood recounting the details of Wednesday’s deadly rail crash, in which at least 68 people were killed and dozens more were injured, wearing a light brown T-shirt stained with the blood of a young American man he had helped move to safety.

Medina and Maia had been in the seventh carriage of the state-operated Renfe train that smashed into the back of a train run by the private Iryo company on the same line from the capital to the south of Spain. Had they been any further forward, they could well have been among the accident’s fatalities.

As it was, the couple climbed out of the train and helped the injured while they waited for medics and Guardia Civil officers to arrive at the scene of the crash, which took place amid vineyards and olive groves near the small town of Urda in the central region of Castilla-La Mancha, near the city of Toledo.

Within hours of the crash, Urda had been transformed into a frantic emergency response centre, with a local sports centre pressed into service as a triage post for the walking wounded. Cars, vans and trucks from the emergency services in Castilla-La Mancha and neighbouring Madrid crowded the streets.

blocks.caption: A member of the Spanish Red Cross embraces a woman as they wait for news of passengers on the two high-speed trains that collided near Urda. Photograph: Susana Vera/Reuters

blocks.text: Fredrich and Arabella Barilea, a couple from the Philippines who now live in Dubai, were on the Iryo train, and Fredrich was sent flying by the impact.

“One guy was shouting, ‘Get out! Get out! Another train could hit!” said Fredrich. “We saw all the people were also getting off. Many of them had head injuries and were covered in blood. We just got as far away from the train as we could.”
Eventually, buses arrived to ferry the lightly injured survivors to Urda – although the Barileas said they were too shocked and confused to know where exactly they had been brought.

“It all happened in a split second,” said Arabella. “The table we were sitting at just disappeared in the crash. I feel like we’re on our second life. You never know what could happen. We’re very grateful.”

blocks.caption: Frederich and Arabella Barilea, originally from the Philippines but currently living in Dubai, were passengers on the Iryo train that the fast train from Madrid hit from behind.  Photograph: Sam Jones

blocks.text: Around the couple, people queued patiently on the street as they waited to board coaches. Wearing torn and bloodstained clothes and, in some cases, bandages on their heads, they stared, mute and uncomprehending. Spain may have been in mourning, as the prime minister, Pedro Sánchez, said during his visit to Urda, but many of those fortunate enough to survive Spain’s second fatal rail crash in less than a year were still too deep in shock to begin grieving.

Ata Yelkaya, a young tourist from Turkey, usually takes the bus when he travels around Spain. On Wednesday, however, he had decided to try the Iryo. Sleepy and assuming his train had come to a halt at a station, he had switched off his tablet and pulled up his hood in preparation for a nap. At 8.53am, he felt what he would later learn was the impact of the Renfe train smashing into the carriages behind him.

“I woke up with a bump and hit my head on the seat in front of me,” he said, “I looked across at an elderly couple near me and saw that the woman had a cut in her eyebrow. That’s when I knew something serious had happened.”

blocks.caption: A passenger rescued from one of the trains involved in the collision in Urda. Photograph: Andrea Comas/AP

blocks.text: When he looked out of the window, he saw the carriages behind his – carriage No 5 – had come off the track and that many people had been killed or injured.

“Everyone was in shock but I tried to help other people get off the train,” he said. “I’m from Turkey and I lived through the 2023 earthquake there, so I stayed calm and tried to think about what to do and how to get out. It was only when I got out and saw some of the dead people that it hit me. I think everyone was in shock; too shocked even to panic or to scream.”

Wednesday’s disaster stirs memories of the Adamuz rail crash in January, in which 46 people died. Once again, a small town has found itself at the centre of a national disaster and, once again, local people have rallied to help, bringing food and water to a hall that had been set up as a centre for those searching for their relatives.

blocks.caption: Medical staff converted a nearby sports centres into a temporary medical facility. Photograph: Andrea Comas/AP

blocks.text: But, as also happened at Adamuz, the solidarity and kindness on display is likely to turn to anger over the coming hours as people seek answers as to how one of Europe’s most modern and extensive high-speed rail networks could experience two deadly accidents that have between them claimed at least 114 lives in the space of just 10 months. With a snap general election just a month away, many voters could use their votes to register their fury over another rail disaster. The “inexplicable circumstances” that led to the crash – as Spain’s transport minister has called them – will need to be explained as swiftly thoroughly as possible.

For all the rush to action and unity on display, there was also a sickening sense of deja vu. One woman from Urda, who had spent the morning driving people to town from the crash site, had few words to describe what she had seen and heard.
“Mejor no verlo,” she said – “it’s better not to see something like this”. Again.

articles.title: SWS: Sara Duterte's defense gets higher net satisfaction than prosecution
articles.summary: Thirty-five percent of adult Filipinos are dissatisfied, while 30 percent are satisfied "that the prosecution of the impeachment case against Vice President Sara Duterte is being done in a just…

blocks.text: Thirty-five percent of adult Filipinos are dissatisfied, while 30 percent are satisfied "that the prosecution of the impeachment case against Vice President Sara Duterte is being done in a just manner," according to a Social Weather Stations (SWS) survey released on Wednesday.
Twelve percent were very satisfied, and 18% were somewhat satisfied. Another 21% were somewhat dissatisfied, and 14% were very dissatisfied. The remaining 36% were undecided.

The September 21 to 27 survey, fielded before the House prosecution dropped three of the four articles of impeachment, yielded a net satisfaction rating of -5 for the prosecution, based on the difference between the percentage of satisfied and dissatisfied respondents.
Meanwhile, 47% of respondents were satisfied with the fairness of Duterte's defense by her lawyers, while 24% were dissatisfied, resulting in a net satisfaction rating of +23.
Background

The Third Quarter 2026 Social Weather Survey was conducted using face-to-face interviews of 1,500 adults nationwide: 600 in Balance Luzon (or Luzon outside Metro Manila) and 300 each in Metro Manila, the Visayas, and Mindanao. The sampling error margins are ±3% for national percentages, ±4% for Balance Luzon, and ±6% each for Metro Manila, the Visayas, and Mindanao.
The survey was non-commissioned.

On October 13, 2026, the Senate impeachment court granted the prosecution’s motion to drop Articles I, III, and IV, leaving only Article II, on unexplained wealth. The defense is scheduled to begin presenting its evidence when the trial resumes on November 9, 2026.
Estrada, Corona trials
According to SWS, net satisfaction with the prosecution is lower than in the trials of then President Joseph Estrada and Supreme Court Chief Justice Renato Corona.
During the Estrada impeachment trial, net satisfaction with the prosecution was +19 (41% satisfied, 22% dissatisfied) in December 2000 and +21 (42% satisfied, 21% dissatisfied) in January 2001.
During the impeachment trial of then-Chief Justice Renato Corona, it was +39 (54% satisfied, 15% dissatisfied) in March 2012.
Except during the Corona trial, net satisfaction was always lower with the prosecution than with the defense, SWS said.
Four accusations
"Asked about the four accusations against Vice President Duterte, more said they do not believe than believe each one, with net belief scores ranging from -9 to -21," SWS reported.
On the misuse of P612.5 million in confidential funds of the Office of the Vice President and the Department of Education, 29% believed it and 38% did not, for a net belief score of -9.
On unexplained wealth that was not fully declared in her Statement of Assets, Liabilities, and Net Worth (SALN), 25% believed it and 38% did not, for a net belief score of -12.
On the bribery of Department of Education officials in connection with procurement irregularities, 27% believed it and 39% did not, for a net belief score of -12.

On the threat to have President Ferdinand Marcos Jr., First Lady Liza Araneta Marcos, and former House Speaker Martin Romualdez assassinated, 23% believed it and 44% did not, for a net belief score of -21.
Around 26% to 30% were undecided on each accusation, while 7% had not heard or read about it, SWS said.
Face the trial
Meanwhile, 78% say it is important for the Vice President to testify personally.

Asked how important it is that Vice President Duterte testifies personally to be able to answer and explain all allegations against her, 78% said it is important: 59% definitely important and 19% somewhat important.
Only 15% said it is not important: 7% somewhat not important and 8% definitely not important. The remaining 8% did not know enough to give an opinion.

SWS said this was similar to the 78% in December 2000 and 79% in January 2001 who said it was important that then-President Estrada testify personally, and to the 73% in March 2012 and 81% in May 2012 who said the same of then-Chief Justice Corona [Chart 8].
"The earlier surveys used a two-point scale (important, not important), so the comparison is only indicative," SWS said. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Montreal grandparent scammer who fled to Central America pleads guilty in U.S. court
articles.summary: Jimmy Ylimaki, a Montreal man accused of defrauding American seniors as part of an elaborate grandparent scam network, has pleaded guilty in a U.S. court.

image.caption: Jimmy Ylimaki, seen here in a photo that appears in a court file in connection with a grandparent scam investigation, has pleaded guilty to participating in a grandparent scam conspiracy. (Matthew Lapierre/CBC)

blocks.text: Montreal
Jimmy Ylimaki, a Montreal man accused of defrauding American seniors as part of an elaborate grandparent scam network, has pleaded guilty in a U.S. court.
Jimmy Ylimaki scammed American seniors as part of an elaborate network
Ylimaki, who was apprehended in Nicaragua earlier this year after spending a year as a fugitive, initially pleaded not guilty to conspiracy to commit fraud.
He changed his plea at a hearing on Oct. 19. He will be sentenced in January and faces up to 20 years in prison.
There are currently 31 other defendants accused alongside Ylimaki. They are being charged in the U.S., but remain in Canada, contesting extradition.

Prosecutors allege that scheme netted tens of millions of dollars. The alleged leader of the scam, Gareth West, appeared to run a real estate investment business, buying and selling property across Ontario and Quebec — while also posing as an influencer and amateur bodybuilder.
Meanwhile, co-conspirators, including Ylimaki, allegedly placed calls to elderly victims at call centres run by West, located around the Montreal area.
On the run in Central America

Ylimaki was caught “red-handed” in one of several raids police conducted against alleged call centres in the Montreal area in June 2024, according to U.S. assistant district attorney Nathanael Burris.
He was placing calls to U.S. seniors in the moments before police arrived. They found him hiding in a downstairs shower, at a building owned by West.
Shortly after the raid, which didn’t immediately lead to charges, Ylimaki left for Costa Rica.

items: Montreal grandparent scammer spent victims' money on cocaine, cars and parties: court documents

blocks.text: Then, in March 2025, police arrested two dozen people in the Montreal area and charged them with fraud-related offences, but West and Ylimaki evaded arrest.
Months later, West was arrested at an Airbnb in Saint-Colomban, Que., in July 2025.
Ylimaki was the only member of the alleged group of scammers who was still at large.
If you know anyone involved in this case, please contact Matthew Lapierre at matthew.lapierre@cbc.ca.
In the summer of 2025, a source with knowledge of Ylimaki's movements told CBC he was living in a coastal city in Costa Rica.
U.S. authorities were also tracking him.

In a motion for detention, filed in March 2026, Burris says Ylimaki — fearing he would be arrested and brought to the U.S. — began researching extradition proceedings involving Costa Rica and learned that the country collaborated with the U.S. on extradition matters. But neighbouring Nicaragua had historically refused U.S. extradition requests.
Tracking a Montrealer with alleged ties to a grandparent scam on the run in Central America
So, he crossed the border, according to Burris's filing.
It did not protect him. In March 2026, U.S. authorities said they had “apprehended” him in Nicaragua and “removed” him to the U.S. The details of that operation remain murky.
Ylimaki was a 'closer'
U.S. prosecutors have said Ylimaki participated in the scam as a “closer” — someone who posed as an attorney representing victims’ family members.
He convinced victims that they needed to provide a large sum of cash, thousands or tens of thousands of dollars, to bail their family member out of jail.
In his role, over just a 67-week period within the alleged three-year conspiracy, Ylimaki was paid more than $367,000 US.

“Moreover, members of the conspiracy in which Jimmy participated frequently transacted in cryptocurrency, making it difficult to ascertain the true extent of Jimmy’s resources,” Burris wrote in his March 2026 filing.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Matthew Lapierre is a journalist at CBC Montreal. He previously worked for the Montreal Gazette and the Globe and Mail. He can be reached at matthew.lapierre@cbc.ca and at mlapierre.07 on Signal.

articles.title: Evacuation from Oleshky: How are preparations going?
articles.summary: A lawyer with the Save Ukraine Foundation, Myroslava Kharchenko, told DW about what has been happening in Russian-occupied Oleshky since a temporary ceasefire brokered by Melania Trump took effect.

image.caption: The view of Russian-occupied Oleshky in Ukraine's Kherson region Image: 34th Separate Marine Brigade "Borysfen"/Handout/REUTERS

blocks.text: Since a ceasefire took effect in the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in Ukraine's Kherson region on October 27, preparations have been underway to evacuate residents trapped there.

Following Russia's occupation of the town in 2022 and the flooding caused by the destruction of the nearby Kakhovka dam in 2023, residents were cut off from the outside world. All access routes to Oleshky, which lies on the Dnipro River, had been mined. Former Oleshky residents who managed to escape and talked to DW described hunger, no access to medicine, and no electricity or water. About 2,000 people are still living in the town.

According to the Save Ukraine Foundation, it has rescued at least 300 civilians from Oleshky over the past six months. DW spoke with lawyer Myroslava Kharchenko, who works for the organization, about preparations for the upcoming evacuation.
DW: A ceasefire is already in effect in Oleshky. Do you know whether any evacuation efforts have begun?

Myroslava Kharchenko: No, we do not have that information yet. What we do know is that the ceasefire came into effect on October 27 at 3 a.m. Kyiv time, which is 4 a.m. in Russia. Mine-clearing operations on the road began at around 8 a.m. What is happening inside Oleshky itself, however, is entirely within the military's remit. Everyone involved in this operation has been asked to maintain strict confidentiality. Any careless remark or action could jeopardize the entire evacuation effort.

What I can see is that information is being actively collected through closed internal local chat groups. Registration lists and application forms are being shared, and people are filling them out themselves. Organizers are contacting those who previously requested evacuation to verify details such as their date of birth and current place of residence. They are also asking people to provide contact information for neighbors or relatives who may be nearby or in the same building, because communications are extremely unreliable.

The organizers are also collecting information about the health conditions of those planning to leave. Among them are people who are ill, have limited mobility, or are recovering from recent injuries, including blast and mine-related wounds. We therefore expect those organizing the evacuation to ensure that medical assistance is available for those who need it.
How exactly is the evacuation expected to take place? Will people be evacuated through Russian-controlled territory or via the Dnipro River? Have any routes already been agreed upon?

As far as we know, a river route would be extremely dangerous. We have not heard any confirmation that such an option has been approved. It therefore appears likely that the evacuation route will pass through the temporarily occupied Ukrainian territory and possibly through Russia before people are able to reach Ukraine. For security reasons, however, none of these details are being made public.
What do you know about the number of people expected to be evacuated?

We are actually very pleased that the evacuation is not expected to take place in a single day. That is important because we hope that those who manage to leave safely during the first stage will serve as an example for others.
People still trapped in Oleshky are extremely afraid. There have already been numerous provocations, and this is not the first attempt to establish such a route or humanitarian corridor.

As a result, there is a great deal of suspicion. Those concerns are based largely on uncertainty, and some people may choose not to leave during the initial phase of the evacuation. Overall, however, we estimate that around 500 people may eventually be evacuated.
Oleshky ceasefire comes into effect in Ukraine war
How would you assess the role of Melania Trump in making this evacuation possible?

We are immensely grateful to Melania Trump for drawing attention to the humanitarian catastrophe currently unfolding in Oleshky. What is taking place there is in fact genocide committed by the Russian Federation.

We are thankful for her efforts and hope they will help make this evacuation possible. We will be even more grateful once most people are safely removed from the combat zone and arrive in Ukrainian government-controlled territory.

blocks.caption: Myroslava Kharchenko from the Save Ukraine FoundationImage: DW Novosti

blocks.text: When could the physical evacuation of civilians begin?

I can't say how long it will take. What seems clear, however, is that time will be needed to clear mines from the roads leading into the city. We also understand that many streets inside Oleshky are mined, so additional work will be required to make routes within the city safe.
There is a hospital from which people need to be evacuated. Nearby is a morgue where bodies also need to be recovered.

I do not know whether that will be included as part of this humanitarian corridor, but it is undoubtedly important. The bodies need to be identified and the causes of death established. That process will also take time, regardless of how quickly the military is able to work.

It is difficult to make any predictions because, as you can see, everything is being conducted under strict secrecy. Statements from both the Russian and Ukrainian sides have been extremely cautious, and that is clearly justified under the circumstances.

articles.title: Netanyahu's bloc leading Israel election but short of majority, partial results show
articles.summary: With 85% of ballots counted, Netanyahu's Likud party and its allies are set to win 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset.

blocks.text: Israel's election result is messy - here's why

Partial results from Israel's general election show veteran Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu is leading his rival, former military chief Gadi Eisenkot, but is still short of a majority in parliament.

With 85% of ballots counted, Netanyahu's Likud party and its far-right and ultra-Orthodox Jewish allies were on track to win 53 seats in the 120-seat Knesset. Eisenkot's Yashar party and three other Jewish opposition parties in his bloc were set for 48.
Both leaders have said they will try to form a governing coalition.
Arab-led parties, who are on course to win an unprecedented 19 seats, could emerge as kingmakers, but all but one of the Jewish parties have pledged not to work with them.
With between 430,000 and 480,000 absentee ballots from soldiers and diplomats yet to be counted, it could still take a day or two for the final election results to emerge.

Once they are confirmed, President Isaac Herzog will hold consultations with all the political factions and invite the leader whom he believes has the best chance of success to form a government - a process that could take weeks.
If they fail, then ultimately there would have to be another election.
During a meeting at his residence in Jerusalem, Herzog praised the 77.7% turnout in Tuesday's election, which was the country's highest in more than two decades.
"It is a badge of honour for Israeli society, and it was remarkable to see how deep the desire for democracy is in Israel," he said.
He added that he expected to receive the official results next week, after which he would begin discussions with every faction.
"We must do everything we can, certainly after yesterday, to avoid another round of elections. So, I expect everyone who comes here to come with an open mind."
Both the prime minister and his main rival have insisted that they should be tasked with forming a governing coalition.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Benjamin Netanyahu called for "a strong right-wing national government"

blocks.text: Image source, EPA
Benjamin Netanyahu called for "a strong right-wing national government"

Eisenkot declared that the public had "spoken in favour of change", after initial exit polls published by three Israeli broadcasters projected that his "Change Bloc" would emerge with between 52 and 53 seats in the Knesset, compared to 50 seats for Netanyahu's bloc.

"The coalition of failure has lost the people's trust," he told supporters at Yashar's election headquarters in Tel Aviv. "I will work with my partners to ensure that the people's decision is translated into a Zionist government."
Later, the broadcasters updated their exit polls, with two projecting that the rival blocs would be tied on 51 seats and one giving Netanyahu's bloc a narrow three-seat lead.
Netanyahu then appeared at Likud's headquarters in Jerusalem and declared that his right-wing bloc had won a "great majority".
"We must put in place a strong right-wing national government," he said. "It is forbidden, simply forbidden, to endanger Israel by forming a government that relies on anti-Zionist Arab parties."

The leader of the left-wing Democrats party told its partners in Eisenkot's bloc on Wednesday that there was an "opportunity to form a change government in partnership" with the Arab parties and replace Netanyahu's coalition.
"We have no future here if we don't stop being afraid. And if we don't put an end to racism," Yair Golan wrote on X.

The two Arab parties - the United Arab List and the Joint List - appear to be heading for record representation because of a strong turnout among Arab Israelis, who account for about a fifth of the population and often describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel.

The chairman of the Joint List, which has talked of providing an electoral "safety net" for the Jewish opposition, said on Wednesday that it was "ready and prepared to pave the way to oust the Netanyahu government".
"Change runs through a Jewish-Arab partnership - a genuine and equal partnership. Nothing less, and nothing more," Yousef Jabareen wrote on X.

blocks.caption: Image caption, Gadi Eisenkot said the Israeli public had "spoken in favour of change"

blocks.text: Image source, Reuters
Gadi Eisenkot said the Israeli public had "spoken in favour of change"

United Arab List leader Mansour Abbas, who served in a short-lived governing coalition formed after the 2021 elections, said on Tuesday night that he hoped "the numbers will work out and we, the Change Bloc and the UAL, can ensure that there are 61 Knesset seats".
Tuesday's election was the first since the deadly Hamas-led attacks on Israel on 7 October 2023 and the wars that followed in Gaza, Lebanon and Iran.

It was also seen by Israelis as one of the most consequential in the country's history, because it could decide not just their leadership but whether the country continues on its current hardline, religious-nationalist trajectory.

Key campaign issues included accountability for the security failures that led to the 7 October attacks, the conduct of regional wars, conscripting ultra-Orthodox Jewish men into the military, judicial reforms and Israel's international standing.

articles.title: Iranian film-maker Jafar Panahi given new prison sentence and has assets seized
articles.summary:
Charges against him are unclear after return to Iran despite being sentenced last year for ‘propaganda activities’

An Iranian court has handed the award-winning film director Jafar Panahi a…

blocks.text: An Iranian court has handed the award-winning film director Jafar Panahi a new prison sentence of five years and one month and ordered the seizure of all his assets.

The 66-year-old, who won the Palme d’Or at Cannes last year for It Was Just an Accident, was sentenced in absentia, his lawyer, Mostafa Nili, told the Iranian news outlet Emtedad. The court also imposed a two-year travel ban and barred him from using social media for two years, Nili said.

The charges against Panahi remain unclear. He returned to Iran in March from an overseas trip to promote It Was Just an Accident, despite having been sentenced in absentia last year to a year in prison ‌for “propaganda activities against the system”.
A friend of the film-maker, an activist based in Europe, told the Associated Press that he had spoken with Panahi on Monday evening after the sentencing and the film-maker had not been detained.

Nili said Panahi currently faced three open legal cases, and had not been notified of the hearing date for the latest one. He only learned of the proceedings after his client’s bank accounts were frozen last week.

Moein Khazaeli, a human rights lawyer at Dadban, a legal counselling centre for Iranian activists, said the sentencing, and the confiscation of Panahi’s assets, could violate Iran’s constitution, unless the authorities establish a clear legal basis linking the property to an alleged offence.
Speaking to the Guardian while in the US earlier this year, Panahi warned that the current “cycle of violence” in Iran could continue.

“What I have been depicting in this film is when the cycle of violence continues, then it becomes very difficult to stop it,” Panahi said. “Unfortunately, because of the savagery that is being carried out by the state, the fear is that this cycle of violence will continue.”
after newsletter promotion
The latest sentence has raised concerns among fellow artists over the risks facing those who continue to work independently in Iran.

The Iranian actor Setareh Maleki, who was forced into exile after starring in Mohammad Rasoulof’s Oscar-nominated film The Seed of the Sacred Fig, told the Guardian: “One of the greatest fears of a dictatorship is losing control over the stories people tell. When those stories cross borders and reach the world, they become impossible to silence. Jafar Panahi has told his stories too, and his sentence proves once again just how deeply the Islamic Republic fears even the act of storytelling.”

Inside Iran, a film-maker currently shooting a film in secret expressed support for Panahi. “We all support him, who brings us great pride. He hasn’t remained silent and instead voices demands of the Iranian people,” said the film-maker, who did not want to give her name.

She said she believed Panahi’s latest sentence was linked to his calls for unity during the January protests and his support for diverse voices inside Iran, including supporters of Reza Pahlavi, the exiled son of Iran’s former shah.

The Iranian-British actor Nazanin Boniadi also condemned the ruling, saying: “Jafar Panahi has spent decades turning censorship into cinematic resistance, bearing witness to the suffering and resilience of the Iranian people. His latest draconian prison sentence is yet another attempt to silence a courageous artist whose work exposes the realities of repression in Iran.”

In a recent report, the US-based Center for Human Rights in Iran warned that Iranian authorities are intensifying their crackdown on artists, writers, poets, musicians and other cultural figures, “pulling peaceful voices into the same coercive security and judicial apparatus used to suppress dissent across Iran”.

articles.title: Tory Brexit was ‘harder’ than promised in EU referendum, says Andy Burnham
articles.summary:
Prime minister warns cabinet not to express opinions about future relationship with Brussels before review of options

Andy Burnham has warned ministers not to express their opinions about…

blocks.text: Andy Burnham has warned ministers not to express their opinions about how the government should approach Brexit, as he argued that the Conservatives’ deal with Brussels had been more extreme than that promised in the 2016 referendum.

In another series of announcements connected to his plan to seek closer links with the EU, Burnham told ministers at a cabinet meeting on Wednesday that the current deal was a bad one, before writing to frontbenchers setting out his hopes to address this.

Brexit was also the main subject of Burnham’s exchanges with Kemi Badenoch at prime minister’s questions on Wednesday, with the prime minister saying the UK had been “paralysed” by the lack of a Conservative plan after the vote.
A Downing Street summary of the cabinet meeting put his comments about Brexit above even those concerning the budget, which the chancellor, John Healey, was to deliver soon afterwards.

“The prime minister opened by setting out how he would shortly write to cabinet on the UK’s relationship with the EU,” it said, adding: “He said the Brexit deal left by the last government had been bad for the UK and had led to a harder Brexit than had been promised at the referendum.”

blocks.caption: Home secretary Shabana Mahmood is among ministers said to be concerned about the implications of a revised Brexit deal. Photograph: James McCauley/Shutterstock

blocks.text: The letter to ministers made similar points, and ended with a warning from Burnham that they should not express opinions about the future shape of relations with the EU before a review of longer-term options.

“It is important that we remain aligned and disciplined as a government in our messaging throughout this period,” he said. “It will not be appropriate for ministers individually to advocate for specific options or opine on the likely outcome of the process.”

It follows reports that some ministers, including Shabana Mahmood, the home secretary, have worries about the idea of a revised deal potentially bringing back the free movement of people to and from the EU, something Burnham has talked up as a possibility.

The letter set out Burnham’s two-stage approach to reforming Brexit, beginning with any initial changes that will stay within Labour’s 2024 manifesto – which committed to remaining outside the EU’s customs union and single market, and not reinstating freedom of movement – a process that will formally kick off when the prime minister attends a European summit next month.
Anything more substantial would need to wait until after the next election, with Burnham saying he wanted a discussion on what this might entail.

“I am clear in my conviction that the Brexit deal negotiated by the Conservative government was not good enough for Britain,” he said in the letter. “It has led to a decade of low growth, burdened businesses with more red tape and weakened our ability to control immigration. It is a harder Brexit than was promised at the EU referendum.
after newsletter promotion

“We hope the summit will lead to some important, concrete steps. Beyond it, we will need to consider the UK’s long-term relationship with the EU as part of our 10-year plan. I will set out the next steps for this process around the summit.

“Both the UK and the EU have changed considerably in the 10 years since the Brexit vote. Any future relationship depends on practical arrangements that are realistic for both sides, and responsive to this new reality.”

Any fundamental changes in the relationship “would be for the public to decide and a matter for the next parliament”, he wrote, adding: “This is government policy to which cabinet collective responsibility applies.”
Challenged by Badenoch at PMQs about his Brexit plans, Burnham reiterated his criticism of the current deal, saying the UK “was paralysed by the party opposite” in the wake of the referendum.
In response, Badenoch said that Burnham had been using freedoms allowed under Brexit, for example, the ability to remove VAT from energy bills: “What he should be saying is: ‘Thank you.’”

articles.title: Canada not in a 'position right now' to agree to U.S. trade deal, Carney says
articles.summary: As trade talks intensify ahead of Tuesday's U.S. midterm elections, Prime Minister Mark Carney says his government will only agree to a deal "when it suits Canadians."

blocks.text: Politics
As trade talks intensify ahead of Tuesday's U.S. midterm elections, Prime Minister Mark Carney says his government will only agree to a deal "when it suits Canadians."
PM says government will agree to deal 'when it suits Canadians'
· CBC News
· Posted: Oct 28, 2026 12:39 PM EDT | Last Updated: 1 hour ago
Canada's not in a 'position right now' to agree to a U.S. trade deal, Prime Minister Mark Carney says.
Prime Minister Mark Carney says his government is not yet in a position to agree to a trade deal with the United States, stressing that an agreement will only be possible "when it suits Canadians."
Speaking to reporters ahead of a Liberal caucus meeting on Wednesday morning, Carney said Ottawa is looking for "the right deal for Canadians."
"We think there's deals that are in the best interests of Canada, first and foremost, but also are in the interests of the United States. That's always been the case. We've been consistent," he said.
"If those deals present themselves, we will pursue them. But we're not at that position right now."
As midterms approach, U.S. teases progress on Canada trade deal
With Canada-U.S. trade tensions emerging as a key issue ahead of the U.S. midterm elections, questions have swirled this week around whether a deal could be reached before the Nov. 3 vote.
U.S. President Donald Trump and other senior American officials have suggested in recent days that progress was being made.
"We'll have ​that settled pretty soon. They're willing to give us anything ​at this moment," Trump said during a rally in Michigan on Sunday.

items: These midterm races will decide who controls U.S. Congress for the rest of Trump's presidency
'I don't know' if Trump would honour a new trade deal: Carney

blocks.text: But while trade talks have intensified, sources told CBC News earlier this week that the conversations didn't mean an agreement was imminent.
A source familiar with the discussions told Radio-Canada that "key elements" of the discussions remain unresolved, adding, "We are not on the verge of an agreement just yet."
Canada-U.S. negotiations fell apart in August and Washington imposed steep tariffs on a range of Canadian goods. Ottawa announced its own "dollar for dollar" levies in response.
Carney was also asked on Monday about the prospects of a deal, saying that his government is ready "to sign an agreement that is in the interests of Canadians."

"We have very clear bottom lines, red lines, which meant that we were not willing to sign what was offered in August," he said. "To the extent to which the U.S. is moving towards accepting those aspects, then there's a greater prospect of a deal."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Jillian Kestler-D'Amours is a senior writer at CBC based in Montreal. You can reach her at jillian.kestler-d.amours@cbc.ca.
With files from Peter Zimonjic, Louis Blouin and Katie Simpson

articles.title: One year on, families seek justice after election violence
articles.summary: One year after Tanzania's deadly post-election violence, families are still seeking answers. A government inquiry recorded 518 deaths. DW research has documented apparent use of excessive force by…

image.caption: The evidence DW has reviewed indicates that police likely acted beyond the scope of their guidelines and trainingImage: AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Warning: This article contains descriptions of violence.
For one family member in Mwanza, Tanzania's second-largest city, justice could begin with a simple act: an apology.
Raha, whose name has been changed for safety reasons, said her nephew, who she raised, was killed during protests that erupted following Tanzania's October 2025 general election.
"The government should have asked for forgiveness for what happened. Even just offering condolences," Raha said.
A year later, the family is still waiting for answers about the death of their loved one.
A disputed election, a deadly crackdown
The violence followed an election campaign marked by the exclusion of the main opposition candidate.

Tundu Lissu, leader of the opposition Tanzanian Party for Democracy and Progress, commonly known as Chadema, had been arrested and charged with treason in April 2025 and his party barred from contesting the election.

blocks.caption: A polling station is set ablaze as clashes erupt in Dar es Salaam on October 29, 2025Image: AFP

blocks.text: On election day and in the days that followed, protesters called for political reforms and the resignation of Tanzanian President Samia Suluhu Hassan.

A government-appointed commission, chaired by retired Chief Justice Mohamed Chande Othman and commonly referred to as the Chande Commission, found that at least 518 people died from "unnatural causes," many from gunshot wounds, and over 2,000 people were injured.
Othman said the death toll could be higher because some families buried their loved ones without taking their bodies to morgues or reporting to the commission.
Human Rights Watch (HRW) also said the actual number of people killed could be higher.
"It's very clear that it's far more than the 518 people that were presented by the commission," said Oryem Nyeko, HRW's senior Africa researcher.
Police likely acted beyond their guidelines
DW analyzed dozens of videos, interviewed sources, reviewed police guidelines and advocacy research, and obtained a leaked police report.

We could not determine the exact location or publication date of every video, as some of the footage was released later due to internet blackouts or anonymously, for fear of reprisals. However, elements in the footage, our sources, public reports, and an internal police report give strong indications that these videos do reveal pieces of what happened in the days following the election.

The evidence DW has reviewed indicates that police likely acted beyond the scope of their guidelines and training. The material reviewed by DW included cases in which people were killed who were not protesting, where protesters were killed by head wounds, and where protesters were beaten or degraded by people in uniform.

The police's specialized Field Force Unit, identifiable in some footage by its red berets and riot-control equipment, helmets, shields and heavy weapons, appeared repeatedly in the material reviewed by DW.

Separately, the Centre for Information Resilience, an open-source investigation organization, documented incidents in Dar es Salaam, Tanzania's biggest city and commercial capital. In one, the uniformed people are beating civilians with sticks. In another, they are located close to where protesters were shot and killed.

DW also identified incidents in which people who were not protesting appear to have been killed. In Mwanza, videos showed the bodies of young men reportedly killed by people in police uniforms while watching television in a video hall. The case was also cited by Human Rights Watch and flagged by the Chande Commission for further investigation.
Who was responsible?

Tanzania's police guidelines restrict the use of firearms to circumstances where they are absolutely necessary. Yet investigations by DW and human rights organizations documented incidents involving protesters with apparent gunshot wounds to the head and upper body and non-protesters shot while trying to flee or while outside during a government-imposed curfew.
Security analyst Nicodemus Minde said the commission left crucial questions unanswered.
"The Commission did not really tell us who was responsible and why," he said.
The presence of a police unit at an incident does not establish who ordered an operation or whether senior officials authorized unlawful force.
The Tanzanian President has described the unrest as an attempt to overthrow the government.
Police violence reports emerge after Tanzania election row
DW confronted the Tanzanian government on the allegations of excessive force by police. The Tanzanian Ministry of Home Affairs declined to comment, saying it would interfere with the legal process.
DW also asked the Tanzanian police for comment. No response had been received by the time of publication.
The Chande Commission recommended further investigation but did not identify security bodies, individual officers or commanders who may have been responsible.
A second inquiry, chaired by retired Justice Shaban Ally Lila, began gathering evidence in August 2026 to further investigate. Its findings are still pending.
'There is no justice'
For the family members of those killed, the inquiries have yet to restore trust.
Zuri, whose name has been changed for safety reasons, said her brother and her son were killed in the post-election violence. She asked why the government had not visited affected families.
"We lost our children; we lost our brothers. Why hasn't the government taken any initiative to at least visit us?" Zuri asked.
"They behave as if nothing happened. Is this justice? There is no justice in Tanzania."
German lawmakers press Tanzania over rights concerns

articles.title: U.S. steel CEO's 'confessions' for buying Stelco prompted government to call its lawyers: industry minister
articles.summary: Canada's industry minister says she called the department's lawyers after the head of Stelco's American parent company told CBC News that he only bought the Hamilton steelmaker to stop it…

image.caption: Minister of Industry Mélanie Joly says she called the government's lawyers to see what the possible consequences are for Cleveland-Cliffs, the U.S. parent company of Stelco, after its CEO Lourenco Goncalves said he bought the company to stop it 'flooding' the U.S. market. (Keito Newman/The Canadian

blocks.text: Politics

Canada's industry minister says she called the department's lawyers after the head of Stelco's American parent company told CBC News that he only bought the Hamilton steelmaker to stop it undercutting his production facilities in the U.S.
CEO buying Stelco to stop undercutting U.S. company 'doesn't look good': trade lawyer
"The last words by the president of Stelco definitely made us contact our lawyers to see what could be the consequences of such confessions," Industry Minister Mélanie Joly said Wednesday.
The minister's comments come after Cleveland-Cliffs CEO Lourenco Goncalves told CBC's Power & Politics Tuesday evening that the Hamilton company was "undercutting our prices in the United States."
"I bought Stelco because I could not afford anymore having Stelco flooding the market here in the United States to the detriment of my own company," he told host David Cochrane.

items: Stelco owner says he could sell plant next year after becoming 'persona non grata in Canada'

blocks.text: The CEO's comments come after Cleveland-Cliffs responded to Joly's recent demands that it reverse layoffs announced last month or face potential legal action for violating Investment Canada Act undertakings.
The government says the company agreed in those undertakings to keep the number of unionized Stelco employees at 2024 levels through to 2029 when the purchase was made.

In a letter to the company last week, Joly said if the company does not honour its agreement with the federal government it would pursue a remedy in the courts. That step, the letter said, could include asking that financial penalties be imposed or an order requiring Cleveland-Cliffs to divest from Stelco.
Stelco in 'full compliance' with commitments to Ottawa, says CEO
Goncalves's company maintains that it's in "full compliance" with the obligations it made under the Investment Canada Act when it bought the steelmaker in 2024.
In a letter to The Canadian Press, Goncalves said he hopes to bring back laid-off Stelco workers before Christmas if a plan to increase Canadian sales succeeds.
The CEO told Power & Politics that he "takes exception" with the notion that he should have to divest from Stelco, saying that, for now, "the company is not for sale," but that will change.

items: Minister gives Stelco owner 15 days to reverse layoffs before turning to the courts

blocks.text: "I will sell the company after we operate the company for a while — and now that I know that I'm persona non grata in Canada, I will do that," he said.

He later said: "Give me another year. I'll make money, sell the company.… [The] minister of industry is not a realtor of companies, and if she is, go sell some other company. This company has an owner, it's Cleveland-Cliffs."
'On the surface it doesn't look good'

Sandy Walker, a lawyer who specializes in competition and the Investment Canada Act, says the Federal Court does have the power order Cleveland-Cliffs to divest itself of Stelco and impose financial penalties of up to $10,000 a day.

She also said Goncalves's comments on Power & Politics raise the question of whether the company signed the Investment Canada Act undertakings in good faith "if he was ultimately planning to shut the company down."
Walker said that while "on the surface it doesn't look good," it's not quite a slam dunk for the government.

items: Will Ottawa really take Stelco to court? Here's what happened last time

blocks.text: Walker said Canada would still have to prove that Cleveland-Cliffs was not subject to conditions beyond its own control when it proceeded with the layoffs.
"I don't think this case is straightforward, that that confession last night is a complete gotcha," she said.
"But it does go to show the attitude of the signatory to these undertakings, assuming [Goncalves] was the one who signed them, and it may go to how hard he is trying to meet those undertakings."
Walker points out that a Canadian court has never made an order to a company under the Investment Canada Act.
In 2009, Ottawa filed a lawsuit against U.S. Steel, after the then owner of Stelco closed many of its Canadian operations when the 2008 financial crisis resulted in a decline in global steel demand.
Ottawa ultimately withdrew the suit in late 2011 when U.S. Steel settled out of court.
Conservative MP urges government to sue Stelco owner
Conservative MP Ned Kuruc, who represents Hamilton-East Stoney Creek, urged the government to sue.
"If the government has an iron-clad contract … file the lawsuit," Kuruc said. "We need action. Get to court, show them we mean business — because ultimately this shows weakness from our government."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Peter Zimonjic is a senior writer for CBC News who reports for digital, radio and television. He has worked as a reporter and columnist in London, England, for the Telegraph, Times and Daily Mail, and in Canada for the Ottawa Citizen, Torstar and Sun Media. He is the author of Into The Darkness: An Account of 7/7, published by Vintage.
With files from Darren Major and Ashley Burke

articles.title: What would a new Israeli government mean for Arab neighbors? More of the same is expected, with some small positives predicted.
articles.summary: A new Israeli government is unlikely to bring big changes on controversial topics like Palestinian statehood and Israeli troops in Lebanon and Syria, experts say. Some small positives may be possible…

image.caption: Arab commentators have celebrated the success of Israel's Arab parties as possible 'kingmakers' in the tight election, including the Joint List (pictured here) — even though most Israeli Jewish parties say they won't govern with them Image: Jamal Awad/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: As Israeli politicians begin to try to build a coalition government, after an election that saw no clear winner, response from politicians in surrounding Arab countries has been muted or non-existent.

This may be because, for the time being anyway, it remains unclear as to whether the new Israeli government will continue with "business as usual" under incumbent Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu or whether a new government headed by Netanyahu's opponents will take what is expected to be a more moderate domestic course.

Whatever the eventual outcome, the consensus is that there is unlikely to be a huge change in Israel's foreign relations with neighboring countries like Syria, Lebanon, Jordan and Egypt, and, further afield, the Gulf states. Nor is it likely to produce very different policies toward Palestinians, which many Arab populations in the region feel strongly about.

blocks.caption: Netanyahu opponent Gadi Eisenkot (pictured), head of the Yashar party, appears to have achieved 16% of the vote. But he will need to build a coalition in order to govern Image: Shir Torem/REUTERS

blocks.text: Both Netanyahu and his main opponent Gadi Eisenkot "are two sides of the same coin," Egyptian politician Mostafa Bakry wrote on X after exit polls seemed to indicate an Eisenkot victory (something that's increasingly contested) and Israeli-Arab parties had displaced Netanyahu's far-right allies. "Arab joy at Netanyahu's near-failure to form the government does not mean that what is to come … differs greatly from his predecessor."

"An Eisenkot government would likely be politically fragile, limiting its room for maneuver," Beth Oppenheim, a policy fellow in the Middle East and North Africa program at the European Council on Foreign Relations, wrote in a commentary last week. "The biggest differences from the current government would be at home: It would halt the judicial overhaul, open a state commission of inquiry into October 7th and pass a conscription law."

However, Oppenheim explained, "when it comes to foreign policy, there would not be a fundamental transformation. Netanyahu's post-October 7th security doctrine — pre-empting threats, operating far beyond Israel's borders and holding 'buffer zones' in neighboring territories — has been embraced by nearly all Jewish Israeli parties."
Palestinian Territories: No two-state solution

One of the election campaign posters for Netanyahu's Likud party bore a stark message — "The right or Palestine" — the message being that if voters did not choose Netanyahu and his right-wing allies, his opponents would be too accommodating toward Israel's Arab-led political parties and would be open to the establishment of a Palestinian state.
But observers believe that message is exaggerated, and that the two-state solution is already dead.

"Support for Palestinian statehood has collapsed across most of the Jewish political spectrum, and permanent Israeli control over Palestinians has become normalized," Oppenheim pointed out. With the exception of one party, "all mainstream Jewish parties support, or at least acquiesce in, the settlement enterprise in some form and publicly oppose a Palestinian state on the 1967 lines."
In August this year, Eisenkot himself said that, "there is no Palestinian state, and no Palestinian state will be established under the government we form."

An Eisenkot-led government would, however, cooperate with more left-wing Israeli parties, which have previously supported a two-state solution. Any new coalition may also need the backing of Israel's Arab-led parties, who are currently thought to have increased their seats in parliament to around 19.

But as Mairav Zonszein, senior Israel analyst at the International Crisis Group, told the news agency Associated Press this week, "At best, [a new government] would be able to slow down the extremely crazy acceleration that we've seen in the last four years of every aspect of Israel's aggression in the occupied territories and inside Israel itself."

A less extreme government would tone down religious messaging, might be less demanding when it came to conditions on disarming Hamas in Gaza, and could potentially move forward with the next stage of the Gaza ceasefire, agreed to in late 2025, but barely implemented. It might also do more to contain settler violence in the West Bank.

blocks.caption: A 2025 survey found that around 82% of Israeli Jews support expelling Palestinains from Gaza (pictured) and around 56% believe Arab citizens of Israel should be expelled Image: Bashar Taleb/AFP

blocks.text: "That's because [settler extremism] is a phenomenon that doesn't enjoy the support of the majority of Israelis, damages Israel's international reputation, and suppressing it is feasible," Elizabeth Tsurkov, a senior fellow at the Washington-based think tank, the Middle East Policy Council, explained on social media.

"[A new Israeli government] would keep expanding the settlements and Palestinian statehood would remain taboo," Oppenheim wrote. "Without a diplomatic track with the Palestinians, further flare-ups of violence in the West Bank and Gaza are inevitable, destabilizing the region — and normalization with Saudi Arabia will remain off the table."
Saudi Arabia: Could anti-Netanyahu bloc bring normalization?

After the October 7, 2023, attack on Israel by Hamas and Israel's ensuing military campaign, which has resulted in at least 70,000 Palestinians killed and Gaza devastated, Saudi Arabia's conditions for normalization with Israel have hardened.
The country, hugely influential in the Muslim world, has put out several statements saying there could be no path to normalizing relations with Israel without some progress on Palestinian statehood.

Last week, at a meeting of foreign ministers from Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Turkey and Egypt, the Saudis co-signed a communique in which the four countries said Israel was "the fundamental source of instability in the region and beyond."

blocks.caption: Video still from a Houthi attack on a Saudi airport in October, 2026. The Saudi government has reportedly rejected Israeli offers of help to fight Yemen's Houthi militia Image: AFPTV/AFP

blocks.text: But there is some cooperation between the two countries behind the scenes. Analysts say that if a government less hardline than Netanyahu's gets into power in Israel, it will be easier for countries like Saudi Arabia — but also the United Arab Emirates, Jordan and Egypt, which all have varying levels of backchannel cooperation and contact with Israel — to admit to this kind of behind-the-scenes diplomacy.
Syria: Security agreement revived?

According to a study published last week by Syrian think tank, Etana, Israeli troops have come as far as 1,160 kilometers (721 miles) into Syria from the two countries' disputed border, occupied Syrian land as far as 400 kilometers from it and carried out 1,996 ground operations in southwest Syria between January and September this year.

Before elections this week there was no chance of any kind of withdrawal from Syria because it would have been seen as "defeat," Ksenia Svetlova, an associate fellow at Chatham House and a former member of the Israeli parliament, told online publication Syria in Transition this month. But if the anti-Netanyahu bloc gets into power, that could change, she suggested.

blocks.caption: Israeli troops have destroyed infrastructure and roads in places like Hamidiyah in Quneitra, near the Golan Heights, in SyriaImage: Ercin Erturk/Anadolu/picture alliance

blocks.text: "A security agreement with Syria will become more probable, as many potential stakeholders [in a new, more centrist Israeli government] have spoken favorably about it in the past," noted Svetlova, who is also director of the Tel Aviv-based Regional Organization for Peace, Economics and Security, which works on Israeli-Palestinian-Arab partnerships. "However I do expect that it will take time as this government will be constantly attacked by the extreme right."

For months this year, Israel and Syrian diplomats negotiated a security agreement under the US' stewardship. But it came to nothing in late 2026 after Israel apparently refused to withdraw back to boundary lines established under a 1974 disengagement agreement.
Lebanon: More diplomacy wanted
Observers and media commentators in Lebanon say the Lebanese government would prefer to have Eisenkot's anti-Netanyahu bloc in power.

Lebanon and Israel are continuing to negotiate an Israeli withdrawal from southern Lebanon, where the Israelis claim they have established a "buffer zone" to facilitate their fight against Lebanese militia group, Hezbollah. The Lebanese argue the Israelis have in fact invaded their country.

And when it comes to negotiations around disarming Hezbollah and withdrawing Israeli troops, there's a perception in Lebanese political circles that Eisenkot would be easier to deal with than Netanyahu and his extremist allies.

blocks.caption: The Israeli military has enormous damage in southern Lebanon. At one stage, Eisenkot accused Netanyahu of giving in to the US when he stopped bombing BeirutImage: Zohra Bensemra/REUTERS

blocks.text: This is despite the fact that Eisenkot is widely seen as the inventor of the so-called "Dahiyeh Doctrine," a military strategy that calls for asymmetric warfare in areas like Beirut's southern suburbs, where Hezbollah is based, to pressure both militants and their civilian support base.
A similar strategy is thought to be being implemented in southern Lebanon now, where whole villages continue to be razed by the Israeli military, even as active fighting has subsided.

Lebanese commentators are also optimistic that Eisenkot, former commander of the Israeli army, would have something in common with their own president, Joseph Aoun, who used to head Lebanon's armed forces.

"When Netanyahu was ousted from power between 2021 and 2022 by Naftali Bennett and Yair Lapid [now members of the camp led by Eisenkot], we were able to negotiate and conclude the maritime agreement," a Lebanese official told Lebanese daily, L'Orient Today, referring to a 2022 deal to share offshore territory.

articles.title: ‘Can’t return home for Undas? Hear mass, pray’
articles.summary: Filipinos unable to return to their provinces on All Saints’ and All Souls’ Days due to high transportation costs can remember the departed by hearing mass and offering prayers, Manila…

blocks.text: October 29, 2026 | 12:00am
Vendors prepare floral arrangements at the Dangwa market in Manila yesterday ahead of All Saints’ and All Souls’ Days.
Edd Gumban, File

MANILA, Philippines — Filipinos unable to return to their provinces on All Saints’ and All Souls’ Days due to high transportation costs can remember the departed by hearing mass and offering prayers, Manila Cathedral vice rector Fr. Vicente Gabriel Bautista said yesterday.

While travel costs could hinder people from going home on Undas, people can “go to parishes in their communities and celebrate mass and after the celebration of the Eucharist, they could pray together as a family and remember them,” Bautista said.
Some Filipinos are mulling canceling their trips to save money as fares have increased due to soaring fuel prices influenced by the Middle East conflict.
Philippine Ports Authority general manager Jay Santiago earlier said they expect passenger traffic at ports during the holiday break to be lower than last year.

Meanwhile, about 2,529 security screening officers of the Office for Transportation Security have had their vacation leaves canceled to ensure sufficient personnel and uninterrupted operations during Undas.– Rudy Santos

articles.title: Broken CCTVs at NAIA flagged
articles.summary: Several closed-circuit television cameras at the Ninoy Aquino International Airport are broken, the Manila International Airport Authority (MIAA) admitted yesterday.

blocks.text: October 29, 2026 | 12:00am

At a Senate public services committee hearing, MIAA assistant general manager Antonio Mendoza confirmed the claim of Frenchman Anthony Claude Boukhors, who had lost a luggage with three luxury watches worth P18 million, at the transport network vehicle service pick-up area at NAIA Terminal 1.
STAR / File
MANILA, Philippines — Several closed-circuit television cameras at the Ninoy Aquino International Airport (NAIA) are broken, the Manila International Airport Authority (MIAA) admitted yesterday.
Attending the hearing virtually from Japan, Boukhors expressed disbelief over the airport’s blind spots.

“I was very surprised some CCTV were not operational, not working. That’s what they told me around airport and in front of Grab and without CCTV not working. And for such a big airport, I was very surprised,” Boukhors said, adding that the pick-up area had “zero cameras.”
Mendoza noted that the airport’s CCTV system is five years old and the New NAIA Infra Corp. (NNIC) has started taking over some of the equipment as part of the transition to privatization.

With the anticipated influx of passengers on All Saints’ and All Souls’ Days, panel chair Sen. Raffy Tulfo issued a 48-hour ultimatum to the MIAA and NNIC to submit a comprehensive status report and ensure all cameras are functioning.
Tulfo said his public service program recovered Boukhors’ three stolen watches.
With a tipster’s help, Tulfo said authorities tracked down the suspect, identified as Raymond Sarmiento, who reportedly sold the P18-million timepieces in Baclaran for P120,000.

articles.title: Wage hikes, livelihood support, health care access pushed
articles.summary: As rising prices, inadequate wages, unemployment and concerns over government accountability continue to weigh heavily on Filipinos, Sen. Bong Go pushed for legislative measures and programs aimed at…

blocks.text: October 29, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — As rising prices, inadequate wages, unemployment and concerns over government accountability continue to weigh heavily on Filipinos, Sen. Bong Go pushed for legislative measures and programs aimed at improving workers’ incomes, expanding livelihood opportunities, protecting public funds and easing the financial burden on struggling families.

Go has emphasized the importance of addressing the everyday concerns of ordinary Filipinos, particularly the rising cost of basic necessities, the need for better-paying jobs, accessible health care and responsible use of government resources.
Recognizing the impact of rising commodity prices on household finances, Go filed Senate Bill 175 or the proposed P100 Daily Minimum Wage Increase Act of 2025.
He also filed the proposed Rural Employment Assistance Program Act and Indigent Jobseekers Assistance Act.
On government accountability, Go has called for transparency and accountability amid the flood control controversy.

articles.title: Hegseth to ASEAN: Deliver peace through strength
articles.summary: United States Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth spoke before his counterparts in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations in Cebu City yesterday, where he reaffirmed the Trump administration’s…

blocks.text: October 29, 2026 | 12:00am

US Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth gestures during a joint press conference with Philippines' Secretary of National Defense Gilberto Teodoro after their meeting at Camp Aguinaldo in Manila on March 28, 2025.
AFP / Ted Aljibe

MANILA, Philippines — United States Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth spoke before his counterparts in the Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) in Cebu City yesterday, where he reaffirmed the Trump administration’s vision for a prosperous and stable Pacific “based on strength, built not on wishful thinking but on the backs of strong, self-reliant nations.”

“The approach we’re taking we describe as strong, quiet and clear. Strong enough to deter coercion and aggression, quiet enough to avoid needless escalation or public theatrics and to let our actions speak for themselves, but are clear enough that our friends, our partners and potential adversaries understand precisely where the United States stands and that we will defend our interests and the interests of our allies and partners,” Hegseth said at opening of the 20th ASEAN Defense Ministers Meeting and 13th ADMM Plus.

“That is by definition peace through strength and we’re ready and willing to work with all of you where you are based on your own circumstances and your own priorities and shared mutual interests thereafter,” he said.

Hegseth noted that while the US and ASEAN member-states are “not going to agree on everything, nor do we need to,” speaking as one on fundamentals “is enough to support practical cooperation where our shared interests are overlapping and are clear, and that’s the type of cooperation the Department of War will continue to pursue with our ASEAN partners.”

He stressed that strengthening maritime domain awareness, improving interoperability and advancing cooperation among US and ASEAN navies are not symbolic things, but “are concrete demonstrations of what serious partners do.”
“Serious partners train together, learn together, plan together and build the confidence and competence necessary to prevent conflict,” he said.

“The United States is a proud Pacific nation, and alongside our ASEAN partners, we are resolved to deliver peace through strength. Peace, prosperity and sovereignty for all member-nations based on mutual respect and strength,” he maintained.

In his remarks, Defense Secretary Gilbert Teodoro Jr. said ASEAN values the United States’ “sustained engagement” with the region’s defense establishments, pointing out that “a robust US presence is necessary for peace and stability in Southeast Asia and in the broader Indo-Pacific region.”
He said the Philippines’ hosting of the ASEAN gathering coincided with the 80th anniversary of the establishment of the Philippines’ diplomatic ties with the US.

In May, Teodoro and Hegseth met on the sidelines of the International Institute for Strategic Studies Shangri-La Dialogue in Singapore to reaffirm their ironclad commitment to the US-Philippine Mutual Defense Treaty and shared determination to ensure a stable peace in the Indo-Pacific.
Meanwhile, Hegseth’s visit was denounced by militant groups, particularly the Bagong Alyansang Makabayan (Bayan), which called him a war criminal undeserving of special treatment in the Philippines.
Bayan secretary general Raymond Palatino said Hegseth should be tried for violating international humanitarian rules in the US war on Iran.

articles.title: Chinese ships monitored near Panatag Shoal
articles.summary: Chinese naval and coast guard vessels and a research ship were spotted near Bajo de Masinloc off Zambales while the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources was distributing fuel to Filipino…

blocks.text: October 29, 2026 | 12:00am

MANILA, Philippines — Chinese naval and coast guard vessels and a research ship were spotted near Bajo de Masinloc (Panatag Shoal) off Zambales while the Bureau of Fisheries and Aquatic Resources (BFAR) was distributing fuel to Filipino fishermen in the area, the Philippine Coast Guard (PCG) reported yesterday.
The PCG, said its spokesman for the West Philippine Sea Rear Adm. Jay Tarriela, monitored the presence of the Chinese vessels on Tuesday while it was assisting the BFAR in its support mission.

“PCG Commandant Vice Admiral Rommel Supangan directed the deployment of PCG surface and air assets to secure the mission, underscoring that the protection of Filipino fishermen and the delivery of government support to them at sea remain among the priorities of the Coast Guard in the West Philippine Sea,” Tarriela said without giving further details.

Some 50 Filipino fishermen around Panatag Shoal received fuel support under the Kadiwa ng Bagong Bayaning Mangingisda Program or KBBM, allowing them to stay longer in the fishing grounds, with reduced fuel costs.
The PCG said the BFAR mission was carried out successfully and with no untoward incidents.
Tarriela underscored that the support missions for the Filipino fisherfolk are aimed at promoting food security and maritime development in the West Philippine Sea.

Flags of the Philippines, the United States and Japan in a composite image.
