MANILA, Philippines — A majority of Filipinos consider the United States and Japan as the Philippines’ most important partners for economic security, a recent survey conducted by Pulse Asia showed.

The Sept. 17 to 23 survey, commissioned by Stratbase ADR Institute, asked the respondents to select from a list up to three countries or organizations that they consider as the Philippines’ most important partners for economic security amid global risks.
The US topped the list with 73 percent of the respondents choosing it among their three, followed by Japan with 62 percent.
Stratbase president Dindo Manhit said the results underscored the Filipinos’ recognition of the role of the United States and Japan in strengthening the Philippines’ economic and strategic position.

articles.title: Digital apps with violent history must prove safety – Angara
articles.summary: Applications with a history of being used for violence should prove their social media platforms are safe for children, Education Secretary Sonny Angara said, amid proposals to ban minors’…

blocks.text: October 29, 2026 | 12:00am
Education Secretary Sonny Angara.
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — Applications with a history of being used for violence should prove their social media platforms are safe for children, Education Secretary Sonny Angara said, amid proposals to ban minors’ access to “high risk digital services.”

“Definitely those apps with a history of being used for violence, being used by terrorists, nihilistic, violent, extremist groups for grooming, we should reverse the burden. Instead of them placing the burden on us to prove that they’re being used for these acts, let’s place the burden on them to prove that their app is safe for the use of our kids,” Angara said.

The Senate has passed on third and final reading the proposed “Safe Media Access and Responsible Technology for Kids in Digital Spaces (SMART KIDS) Act,” seeking to ban minors’ access to “high risk digital services” like Roblox and GoreBox, which are online platforms where youth have been groomed into committing violent acts.
Angara said he is in favor of measures regulating internet use for minors.

“I don’t know which age, we’ll leave it to our legislators, but definitely, I think up to 15, 16, very vulnerable for them because they’re very emotional and their faculties are not fully formed. And then also, because they’re very emotional, sometimes they do something and they regret later on,” Angara said.
The bill will compel high-risk digital services to suspend, restrict, disable or remove any account owned, operated or used by anyone under 18 years old.

Not covered by the ban are electronic mail services, private messaging services, online gaming services not primarily used for social networking, educational platforms, news services and professional collaboration services.
“Because there may still be technology in educational apps and maybe communication apps,” he said.
Angara said that implementation is crucial once the proposed measure is signed into law.
“The enforcement is also something that should come into play when you pass a law because that will be partially or wholly unenforceable,” he said.

articles.title: Bernardo: Jinggoy got P573 million in kickbacks in 4 tranches
articles.summary: Former public works undersecretary and state witness Roberto Bernardo testified yesterday before the Sandiganbayan that detained Sen. Jinggoy Estrada received P573 million in kickbacks, delivered in…

blocks.text: October 29, 2026 | 12:00am
Sen.Jinggoy Estrada leaves the Sandiganbayan in Quezon City after attending his scheduled arraignment on the graft case filed against him at the Sandiganbayan in Quezon City on June 2, 2026.
STAR / Miguel de Guzman

MANILA, Philippines — Former public works undersecretary and state witness Roberto Bernardo testified yesterday before the Sandiganbayan that detained Sen. Jinggoy Estrada received P573 million in kickbacks, delivered in four tranches, from infrastructure projects.
During the bail hearing of Estrada’s plunder case, Bernardo said the money was delivered from the Diamond Hotel in Manila to Estrada’s residence in San Juan.

The first delivery was in November 2024, the second in December 2024 and the third and fourth in February 2025. For the final delivery, Bernardo said he accompanied his driver in bringing 11 boxes containing P20 million to the senator’s residence.
He, however, said he has no photographs of the alleged transactions, saying he was aware that these were “illegal” and he did not need to provide documents or evidence.
Implicating a friend
During the hearing, Bernardo was asked why he did not initially name Estrada among the officials who allegedly received kickbacks in his affidavit in September 2025.
He only later accused Estrada of receiving kickbacks from infrastructure projects in November 2025 and his latest judicial affidavit on Monday.
Bernardo cited his friendship with Estrada, saying even though he already knew that the senator was a proponent of projects, he wanted to have solid evidence first before implicating a friend.
“It was difficult to implicate a friend. I couldn’t do it right away,” he said.
Bernardo pointed out that he reserved his right to execute a supplemental affidavit, if needed, due to the complex nature of the case.
Estrada personally attended the bail hearing for the first time, then asked the Sandiganbayan to allow him to return to his cell at the New Quezon City Jail in Payatas.
Asked for comment on Bernardo’s testimony, Estrada said it has a lot of inconsistencies. “He implicated too many people. The testimony is full of inconsistencies.
It was clear that he never brought money to me,” said Estrada.
When asked if he considered Bernardo a friend before, the senator said he did not want to have enemies as much as possible.

articles.title: DBM: NCA utilization rate at 96.6%
articles.summary: Government agencies utilized 96.6 percent of their notices of cash allocation (NCA) as of end-September, while the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) had the largest amount of unused NCAs…

blocks.text: October 29, 2026 | 12:00am
Data from the Department of Budget and Management (DBM) showed that NCAs grew by 7.5 percent to nearly P4 trillion as of end-September from P3.72 trillion in the same period last year.
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — Government agencies utilized 96.6 percent of their notices of cash allocation (NCA) as of end-September, while the Department of Public Works and Highways (DPWH) had the largest amount of unused NCAs at P59.19 billion.
Even with the increase, government agencies recorded a slightly lower utilization rate of 96.6 percent from 97.3 percent in the nine months in 2025.
This means that of the total releases, P3.86 trillion has been utilized and some P136.5 billion was unused as of end-September.

NCAs are disbursement orders by the DBM to government banks servicing the release of funds to agencies. State agencies are expected to use the NCAs to pay for the cash requirements of their programs and projects.
Line departments, which received the bulk of the releases, registered a utilization rate of 95.2 percent from 96.6 percent last year. They used P2.6 trillion of the P2.73 trillion released.
This leaves P130.6 billion in NCAs for the period.
By department, the DPWH had the biggest unused NCAs as of end-September.
The DPWH recorded a utilization rate of 86.7 percent from 95.6 percent last year. It used P386.07 billion of the P445.26 billion released.

The DPWH is facing stricter scrutiny over the release and use of funds after being embroiled in multibillion-peso irregularities in flood control projects, which prompted an overhaul of its leadership and budget and even procurement processes.
The Department of Education (DepEd) received the largest allocation among departments at P624.3 billion, of which P601.57 billion or 96.4 percent had been utilized.
Those that had full utilization rates include the judiciary, Commission on Audit, Commission on Elections, Office of the Ombudsman and the Commission on Human Rights.
Among agencies with lower utilization rates is the Department of Agriculture, which posted an 84.8 percent rate after using P70.11 billion of its P82.64-billion NCA allocation.

Others are the Department of Information and Communications Technology (85.1 percent rate), Civil Service Commission (81.4 percent), Office of the President (76.3 percent) and Presidential Communications Office (75.3 percent).

articles.title: PNP launches hotlines for tipsters on Bato
articles.summary: The Philippine National Police has opened five 24/7 hotlines and guaranteed confidentiality for tipsters who can provide any information on the whereabouts of wanted Sen. Ronald “Bato”…

blocks.text: October 29, 2026 | 12:00am
Police display on screen the hotline numbers to receive information on Sen. Ronald dela Rosa’s whereabouts. (Inset) Senator Bato Dela Rosa.
STAR / File

MANILA, Philippines — The Philippine National Police has opened five 24/7 hotlines and guaranteed confidentiality for tipsters who can provide any information on the whereabouts of wanted Sen. Ronald “Bato” dela Rosa.

PNP spokesman Col. Allen Rae Co said the cellphone numbers are 0927-3073501, 0995-5122729, 0945-6115926, 0999-3619878 and 0960-6923025. They are operational and ready to accept calls and messages from informants who have leads on Dela Rosa.
Co added that tipsters can also use the Unified 911 hotline.
“We assure anybody who will be giving tips that their identities, numbers will be kept confidential,” Co said at a news briefing in Camp Crame.
Dela Rosa is believed to be hiding somewhere in Mindanao under the protection of a powerful armed group.

With the looming deadline for Dela Rosa to surrender, Co urged members of the senator’s family to convince him to turn himself in to the authorities, adding that they want a peaceful resolution and accord the senator dignity instead of hunting him down.
“Maybe they could talk to the senator and prevail upon him to voluntarily surrender,” Co said.
If the senator’s wife Nancy would reach out to them, Co said they would welcome the gesture.
Another person who could serve as a bridge is Dela Rosa’s son, Rock, a captain in the police force.
“It’s very hard for a son but that’s one of the avenues,” he said.
‘No political persecution’

Efforts to track down Dela Rosa do not constitute political persecution, Malacañang stressed yesterday. ?Palace press officer Claire Castro said Dela Rosa’s case started in 2017 during the term of former president Rodrigo Duterte, whose controversial drug war left more than 6,000 suspects dead based on official data.

“At that time, President Marcos Jr. was a private citizen. To claim that it is a political persecution is a bit far-fetched,” Castro told Bombo Radyo yesterday. ?Castro cited Republic Act 9851 or the Philippine Act on Crimes Against International Humanitarian Law, Genocide and Other Crimes Against Humanity to justify the operations against Dela Rosa, who was chief of the PNP when Duterte launched the drug war.

Under the law, authorities may surrender or extradite suspected or accused persons in the Philippines to an appropriate international court, if any, or to another state pursuant to the applicable extradition laws and treaties.
“We did not violate any law,” Castro said.

“If this issue did not happen way, way back, the government would not surrender anyone. It just happened that there is an issue and let us not forget that there are alleged victims of EJK (extrajudicial killings) who also need justice,” she added.

Castro responded to critics who argued that no local institution has issued an arrest warrant against Dela Rosa and that surrendering the senator to the ICC is tantamount to turning over a Filipino citizen to foreigners.
She argued that the ICC is a court, not a foreign state, and that the Philippines was a member of the ICC when the case started.

“Let us not just focus on Sen. Bato and other co-perpetrators. Let us also remember as Filipinos that there are Filipinos who are crying and who have ill feelings because they feel that they have not receive enough and real justice,” Castro added.
The government has offered a P50-million bounty for the capture of the senator and has given him until tomorrow to surrender. – Alexis Romero

articles.title: Ukraine's Zelenskyy irked by US-Russia-China summit
articles.summary: Volodymyr Zelenskyy has voiced his concerns about a probable meeting between the leaders of the US, China and Russia next month. Plus, a localized truce appeared to be holding in the town of Oleshky.

image.caption: Zelenskyy is concerned that Xi Jinping, Donald Trump and Vladimir Putin could divide up global spheres of influence between themImage: Dmitri Lovetsky/AP Photo/picture alliance

blocks.text: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has warned that a planned meeting between Russia, China and the United States next month could present the three participants with an opportunity to redraw global spheres of influence.

"We really don't want this to turn into 'Yalta 2, 3, 4' with a redistribution of influence," he said in comments to journalists on Wednesday, referring to the 1945 Yalta Conference in Crimea , where Allied powers redrew the world map in the wake of the Second World War.
Putin raised idea of three-way summit with Trump: What to know

The Kremlin has previously indicated that preparations were underway for a meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin and his US and Chinese counterparts, Donald Trump and Xi Jinping, on the sidelines of an Asia-Pacific summit next month.
The Wall Street Journal first broke the news about the three-way summit earlier this month and said that Trump had not agreed to attend the summit at the time.
But the Journal said Trump was open to the proposal — that had been raised by Putin — since he wanted to bring an end to the war in Ukraine.

"What China, Russia and the United States might discuss has not yet been clearly defined," Zelenskyy said, adding that "Russia wants this meeting more than anyone," warning against handing Moscow "another major diplomatic advantage."
For years now, Russia has been seeking a new agreement with Washington on European security architecture, and in particular an end to what Putin considers NATO's aggressive expansion towards Russia.
Putin has falsely repeatedly said Ukraine war was an act of self-defense
Putin continues to cast the ongoing invasion of Ukraine as a response to such a NATO threat – a position widely rejected in Kyiv and the rest of Europe.
Zelenskyy's warning came ahead of planned talks between Ukrainian, Russian and US envoys in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) next month.
No specific date has been set for the Abu Dhabi meeting, but Kyiv is keen for it to take place before the potential Russia-China-US summit.
Before that, it was also confirmed on Wednesday that Russian Foreign Minister Sergey Lavrov will travel to the United States for a meeting with G20 counterparts in Atlanta on October 30-31.

blocks.caption: Zelenskyy's comments were released as he traveled to the Netherlands for talks with Dutch Prime Minister Rob JettenImage: Remko de Waal/ANP/picture alliance

blocks.text: Zelenskyy in Netherlands
Zelenskyy's remarks were released as he traveled to the Netherlands for meetings with Dutch Prime Minister Rob Jetten and Dutch King Willem-Alexander in The Hague.
The Dutch government said on Wednesday it would provide Ukraine with €1.2 billion ($1.3 billion) in non-military support over the next ⁠years.
Zelenskyy also held a phone call with British Prime Minister Andy Burnham to thank him for an ​extra £10 ⁠billion ($13.29 billion/€11.94 billion) of support announced earlier ⁠on ​Wednesday.
"A truly ​strong very timely step coming right Russia needs to and ​feel that Ukraine will not be left ​alone to deal with the problems ⁠Russia ​is so ​eager to escalate," he wrote on social media.
But Ukraine's greatest assets in its defense against Russian aggression remain US Patriot air defense missiles, and Zelenskyy urged Washington to increase supplies.
Zelenskyy said Ukraine had been receiving 12 missiles a month this year but is being targeted with "150 ballistic missiles a month."
Oleshky truce holding for now, Zelenskyy says
Meanwhile on the battlefield, officials said a six-day ceasefire in a Russian-occupied town in southern Ukraine held for its first day and night.

The localized truce in the devastated town of Oleshky began on Tuesday and is due to last until Sunday, enabling a planned humanitarian operation to provide around 2,000 remaining residents with urgently needed food and medicine, and evacuate those who want to leave.
"We are grateful that they are organizing this possibility to evacuate people," said President Zelenskyy.
The plight of Oleshky in Ukraine's southern Kherson region caught the attention of US first lady Melania Trump, who the White House said helped broker the humanitarian mission.
If the ceasefire holds, it will be the first time in more than four-and-a-half years of fighting that both sides have observed a significant truce, with previous attempts quickly unraveling.
"This is the biggest de-escalation since 2022," said Ukraine's negotiator, Davyd ‌Arakhamia, on Tuesday, adding every step brings peace closer.
Oleshky ceasefire comes into effect in Ukraine war
Drone attacks in Kharkiv, Belgorod — and off Bulgaria
Elsewhere, however, the war raged on with five people, including a four-year-old child, injured in a Russian drone strike on the northeastern Ukrainian city of Kharkiv overnight.

In Moscow, the Russian Defense Ministry said air defenses had downed 531 Ukrainian drones on Tuesday night and into Wednesday morning, but local authorities in the Belgorod border region said one person was killed in a drone attack.
And in Sofia, Bulgarian Defense Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said three maritime drones struck a container ship in the Black Sea off the coast of Bulgaria.

The crew evacuated the vessel and there were no immediate reports of casualties, according to Bulgarian state news agency BTA, but the incident took place as defense ministers from Bulgaria, Romania and Turkey were meeting in Sofia for trilateral talks focused on Black Sea security.

"We follow with concern the intense attacks on commercial vessels in the Black Sea ​and call on the sides to act with common sense, in line with the principle of navigational safety in open seas," said Turkish Defense Minister Yasar Guler.
"The necessary warnings are constantly being conveyed to both sides to keep commercial navigational out of the conflict zone and ​immediately halt attacks on civilian vessels."
A series of drone attacks have occurred this month off the coasts of NATO members Romania and Bulgaria. Russia has not taken responsibility, but suspicion has increasingly fallen on Moscow.
"The logic points in that direction," Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev told parliament earlier this month. "The problem is that we cannot prove it."

articles.title: Flavio Bolsonaro lands in US, declares himself 'leader' of Brazil
articles.summary: Defeated Brazilian presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro and his family landed in Florida early on Wednesday. Facing money laundering allegations, he fled just days after refusing to concede defeat…

image.caption: News of Bolsonaro departing Brazil broke on Tuesday, just two days after Brazil's presidential electionsImage: Ricardo Arduengo/AFP

blocks.text: Brazilian right-wing presidential candidate Flavio Bolsonaro and his family landed in Miami, in the US state of Florida, on Wednesday morning.
His plan to leave Brazil became public knowledge late on Tuesday, soon after he had refused to concede defeat in Sunday's presidential elections and pledged to challenge the results.

Bolsonaro refused to comply with a Brazilian Supreme Court order to surrender his passports, tied to a money-laundering investigation in which he denies wrongdoing, and the US State Department later said it would grant him and his family visas.

blocks.caption: The Bolsonaro's were escorted to a vehicle under cover of umbrellas Image: Eva Marie Uzcategui/REUTERS

blocks.text: Bolsonaro declares himself president-elect of Brazil despite losing election
Hours after arriving in the US, Bolsonaro declared himself the rightful president-elect of Brazil and said he had left the country so he could be the leader "my people deserve."
He later altered a message to call himself the "leader" of Brazil rather than "president-elect."
He said that his victory had been denied by an electoral coup d'etat by ‌leftist President Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva and the country's Supreme Court.
The right-wing senator said he would lead the opposition from the US.

"I want to say, not only to my 60 ‌million voters but to the Brazilian people, that ‌I ​am the elected president and that the criminals who stole Brazil's election are part of a criminal organization that has established a ​tyranny," he said in an open letter shared with journalists by his allies.
Bolsonaro did not provide evidence for ⁠the ​alleged electoral fraud. International observers have ​found Sunday's voting was fair.
Flavio Bolsonaro flees to the US from Brazil
When did Bolsonaro arrive and how did he reach Miami?
Bolsonaro, his wife and two daughters were seen disembarking a Gulfstream G400 plane and heading into the Miami-Opa Locka airport on Wednesday morning.
Their journey across the Americas had captured regional attention.
The quartet first flew into Argentina late on Tuesday, then took a private jet to the Ecuadorian city of Guayaquil. From there, they continued to Miami, in Florida.

Bolsonaro would lose his immunity from prosecution in February when his term in the Senate ends. On Monday, he had said in an Instagram post that he had no intention of leaving the country and that he would "hand over my passports and defend myself against this travesty, which is a clear attempt to intimidate me."
According to the AFP news agency, Bolsonaro also holds Italian citizenship and so was able to travel despite his Brazilian and diplomatic passports being canceled.

blocks.caption: Bolsonaro's flights out of Brazil and towards Miami had been tracked overnightImage: Eva Marie Uzcategui/REUTERS

blocks.text: Potential source of strain between Trump's US and Lula's Brazil

Bolsonaro's departure and his arrival in Florida — like his father Jair Bolsonaro before him after Brazil's previous presidential elections — could deepen a rift between the two most populous countries in the Americas.
During the election campaign, incumbent president Lula had accused the Donald Trump administration of colluding with the Bolsonaro family in a bid to help them return to power.

After the election results, Trump appeared to question the integrity of the vote, saying he thought the extension to voting times was a "very bad look." He had also alleged in the past that Jair Bolsonaro was the victim of judicial persecution in Brazil.
Bolsonaro senior is now in jail in Brazil on charges of leading a conspiracy designed to keep him in power despite defeat in 2022's presidential election.
Brazil's Lula celebrates election victory as Bolsonaro rejects results

articles.summary: With 85% of votes counted, all signs point to an impasse. The most likely outcome may be new elections.

blocks.text: Could Netanyahu persuade Eisenkot to join him in a national unity government?
Eisenkot would have to abandon his key platform to do so. He's framed himself as the only alternative to Netanyahu, and built his campaign on ousting him from power.

Just last night, he took to the stage at his campaign HQ and called on Netanyahu to "announce his retirement from political life today," telling the crowd that Israelis are fed up with Netanyahu's "culture of lies", "division and incitement".
But that was before one of the main exit polls - which had initially projected a lead for Eisenkot's bloc - was revised, and he was overtaken by Netanyahu.

Netanyahu could try to persuade Eisenkot's Yashar Party to join his Likud Party in a unity government by ditching the far-right and ultra-Orthodox parties he is currently in coalition with. But last night at Likud HQ he thanked his "loyal partners" and called for a "strong right-wing government"- remarks some have interpreted as meaning he intends to preserve his alliance with them.

One thing that could make a unity government more likely is a renewed conflict with Iran, which could place serious pressure on party leaders to put aside their political differences and work together. In the days prior to the election, Israeli and US media reported that Netanyahu was pushing for fresh strikes on the country, and had pressed Donald Trump to approve US involvement.
This would no-doubt be framed by Netanyahu's critics as an attempt to save his own political skin by entering another regional conflict.
This would be a seismic shift for Israeli politics. Only one independent Arab party has ever formally been part of a coalition, in 2021, and it didn't last long.
Eisenkot and every other Jewish party in his bloc bar one have already ruled out entering government with them. But right now, it's the opposition's only path to a majority.

The Arab parties were the story of election night. They look to have defied expectations and could gain a record 19 seats - helped by an unprecedented turnout from Israel's Arab population, who account for about one-fifth of the country and often describe themselves as Palestinian citizens of Israel.

For years, many boycotted Israeli elections, saying voting would legitimise a system that they say treats them as second-class citizens. But their turnout last night, inspired by a desire to oust the most right-wing governing coalition in Israel's history, has shaken things up.

The United Arab list, who are currently projected to win around 7 seats, have said they'd join an opposition government, while The Joint List, who are projected to win 12 seats, have said they'd support one from outside.

However, the only Jewish leader advocating this scenario right now is The Democrats' Yair Golan. And a coalition like this would be very fragile, especially on issues like Gaza and the occupied West Bank.
The fact there is such a unified front from the Jewish parties against Arab participation points to Israel's deep divisions.

articles.title: Second fatal train collision this year casts doubt over Spain’s high-speed rail network
articles.summary: Questions were raised before Toledo crash over rail safety in a country where train travel has surged by 40%

blocks.text: Spain’s high-speed rail network, the most extensive in Europe and the second largest in the world after China, has long ranked as a point of pride in the country. But Wednesday’s deadly crash – the second in nine months – has recast the spotlight on questions about safety.
Officials said at least 64 people were killed on Wednesday morning after two trains collided, leading to the derailment of several carriages. The two trains were carrying 544 passengers.

While the cause of the accident has yet to be confirmed, a source told Reuters that a train operated by the private company Iryo had come to a halt near the city of Toledo because of a signalling fault and on orders from infrastructure manager Adif. Soon after, a second train, operated by state-owned Renfe struck the stationary train. It had been travelling on the same line at a high speed.
Renfe said in a statement that its train had been instructed to continue on its way and had crashed into ​the stationary Iryo train “for reasons we don’t know”.
The accident follows a crash in January that killed 46 people and left dozens more injured near the town of Adamuz in Andalucía.

blocks.caption: A Guardia Civil officer collects evidence at the site of January’s fatal rail crash near Adamuz in Andalucía. Photograph: Manu Fernández/AP

blocks.text: Media on Wednesday were swift to point to the parallels between the two crashes: both involved the same train operators and took place on the line connecting Madrid to the southern region of Andalusia, which is the oldest on Spain’s high-speed network.
The first crash sparked a wider conversation over safety on the line, a debate that rail unions say has continued.

Wednesday’s disaster came a day before a planned 24-hour work stoppage at Renfe by Spain’s largest train drivers union. “Our goal is to change the system and make it safer,” the union said earlier this month.

Their reasons for taking action ranged from the need for climate emergency protocols to ensuring channels of communication for workers to convey concerns. The union also called for guarantees that trains would be “reliable and safe”, adding: “We demand real and definitive technical solutions to the safety and reliability issues that have long plagued our rolling stock.”
It has also called a rolling, six-day strike for drivers at the high-speed rail operator Ouigo.

The January crash sparked a bout of political finger-pointing over whether Pedro Sánchez’s Socialist party government had spent enough on railway maintenance in a country where travel by train accounts for about 57% of all transport.

Train travel grew by 40% from 2019 to 2024, coinciding with a period in which the country opened up its rail network to private companies. In the first half of this year, 25 million passengers used a high-speed train in Spain.
The government says it has increased spending on railway network maintenance by 54% since taking power in 2018.

blocks.caption: The aftermath of the 2013 crash near Santiago de Compostela that claimed 80 lives. It remains Spain’s worst rail disaster.  Photograph: Reuters

blocks.text: Spain spends more than any other country on its high-speed network, averaging about €1.5bn (£1.26bn) a year from 2018 to 2022, according to a Reuters analysis of EU data. More than 90% of Spain’s train network is equipped with the highest level of safety control systems in the EU.
Much of the funding, however, has seemingly been directed at new infrastructure, with about 16% earmarked for maintenance, renewal and upgrades.

Data from the European Commission suggests Spain’s maintenance investment in its 4,000km (2,500 miles) of high-speed lines has lagged behind countries such as Germany or Switzerland although some of this could be attributed to differences in the age of the rail lines and the cost of public works and materials.

Until this year, Spain had among the lowest accident rates in the EU, with just one or fewer fatalities per thousand kilometres of track, according to data from Eurostat, the statistics arm of the EU.
Spain’s worst rail accident took place in 2013, when 80 people died after a train veered off a curved section of track outside the north-western city of Santiago de Compostela.

articles.title: Philip Lustre seeks transfer of cyber libel case from Davao City
articles.summary: The camp of veteran journalist Philip Lustre Jr., on Wednesday said they will ask that the cyber libel case against him be transferred from Davao City.

blocks.text: Published October 28, 2026 10:23pm
The camp of veteran journalist Philip Lustre Jr., on Wednesday said they will ask that the cyber libel case against him be transferred from Davao City.

“For the court, we are in the course of filing the necessary pre-arraignment remedies including a motion for reinvestigation, motion to quash, and to of course transfer the venue because we do not feel safe in Davao City,” Lustre's lawyer Dino De Leon said in a press briefing.
He added that this is “considering the known proclivity of the Duterte family for violence.”
Police officers arrested Lustre in Quezon City on Saturday on the strength of a cyber libel arrest warrant issued by a court in Davao City.
De Leon later said that the complainant is lawyer Manases Carpio, the husband of Vice President Sara Duterte.
Lustre has been temporarily released after posting bail.
De Leon said he has also asked Davao City Prosecutor Jhopee Avanceña to confirm her ties to Honeylet Avanceña, the partner of former president Rodrigo Duterte.
National Bureau of Investigation Director Melvin Matibag earlier said that Jhopee Avanceña and Honeylet Avanceña are cousins.

“Kami talaga ay nagugulat na pinirmahan niya ito kung related talaga siya kay Honeylet na kinakasama, longtime partner, in fact the de facto first lady nung mga panahon ni Rodrigo Duterte,” De Leon said.
(We are really surprised that he signed this, if he is indeed related to Honeylet, his live-in partner, longtime partner, and in fact, the de facto first lady during Rodrigo Duterte’s time.)
“We are asking for the record and, formally, we already wrote to the city prosecutor to confirm his relationship with Honeylet Avanceña,” he added.
He said they are also asking the prosecutor’s office for proof of service that subpoenas and summons were sent to Lustre.
De Leon said they are also asking the prosecutor’s office to show the efforts made to determine Lustre’s correct address.

Lustre’s camp previously said it was looking into what appeared to be a violation of his right to due process during the preliminary investigation, as he had neither been served nor received a subpoena or notice.

Prosecutor General Richard Fadullon also said that Lustre was denied due process because he was not given the opportunity to respond to the complaint before an arrest warrant was issued against him. — BM, GMA News

articles.title: Is Iran headed to war or peace after Mecca alliance meeting?
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey have taken their latest peace push directly to Tehran. Officially, it was to avert a new military escalation, but their diplomatic outreach can also be seen as a…

image.caption: Senior officials from Turkey, Pakistan and Saudi Arabia all traveled to Tehran to meet President Masoud Pezeshkian and other Iranian leadersImage: Iranian Presidency/AFP

blocks.text: Amid rising fear that the US and Israel are preparing to launch new attacks on Iran after the US midterm electionon November 3, three major Middle Eastern powers delivered a coordinated diplomatic message directly to Tehran.

Pakistan's army chief Asim Munir, Saudi Defense Minister Khalid bin Salman and Turkish intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin all traveled to Iran to meet Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian and senior officials in Tehran this Monday. The three envoys serve as representatives for the Mecca defense pact — a military alliance of Islamabad, Riyad and Ankara, which was officially set up this summer.
Saudi Arabia said ⁠the ⁠trip aims to open negotiating channels and "prevent the return of military escalation." Details on the agenda, however, remain scarce.
Iran conflict: Could a new phase of the war be imminent?

A senior Pakistani official cited by the Reuters news agency said the talks focused on building a regional non-aggression network, in addition to US-Iran talks, Houthi rebels' attacks on Saudi Arabia, the Strait of Hormuz and the US naval blockade.

Another official said Pakistan's Munir presented Iran with a solution to the conflict that would offer something both to Washington and Iran, with the three Mecca states and Qatar acting as mediators. The source told Reuters US President Donald Trump previously gave Munir the go-ahead to try diplomacy.
Tehran presents the meeting as a success
Iran hailed the "very positive atmosphere" during the Tehran talks, even though no breakthroughs were officially announced.
"Very good discussions took place between us," Mohsen Rezaei, head of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, told state television. "I feel that a new atmosphere is emerging in the region."
Rezaei argued that regional security should be built by countries in West Asia themselves and without outside intervention.

A day later, Rezaei reportedly met Supreme Leader Mojtaba Khamenei. Iranian state media said Khamenei called for protecting Iran's interests and maintaining Tehran's conditions for ending both the war and the current state of "neither war nor peace."

Meanwhile, Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian travelled to Moscow for the Gas Exporting Countries Forum, where he met Russian President Vladimir Putin and Qatar's Emir Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al Thani, with Pezeshkian and the emir also discussing the war and the Strait of Hormuz.
These and other diplomatic contacts were framed by Tehran as evidence that the US is unable to diplomatically isolate the Iranian regime.
Are Turkey and Pakistan closing ranks with Saudi Arabia?

The united front presented by the three nations in Tehran, however, can also be seen as a show of force for the new Mecca defense alliance. It comes as the Saudis grow increasingly wary of the attacks on Saudi infrastructure launched by the Iran-allied Houthi militants.
Egypt ready to back Saudi Arabia's war against Houthis

Under the terms of the Mecca agreement, an outside attack on one of the member states is to be regarded as an attack on all of them. The visit also came on the same day as Egypt's parliament agreeing to give military help to Ryad and take "all necessary measures" to help Saudi Arabia defend itself, in addition to the looming threat of the US and Israel.

"The presence of the three senior representatives at the same time sent the message that these countries are acting as a bloc," Babak Dorbeiki, a London-based political analyst and former official at Iran's Strategic Research Center, told DW.

Saudi Arabia has long been regarded as Iran's archrival in region. It has used its enormous wealth to counter Iran's influence, and now it can, at least in theory, also count on Pakistan's nuclear capability, and Turkey's conventional military strength.
At the same time, Dorbeiki argued that the Mecca pact is primarily designed for deterrence rather than offensive war. And defense pact does not mean its members want to fight Iran.
Dorbeiki believes the message from the bloc could therefore work in two directions: it can provide mediation, but continued escalation could also alter that position.
Ryad pushing for a 'diplomatic solution'

Saudi Arabia faces the most immediate dilemma. Further Houthi attacks damage its infrastructure and economy, but a wider war with Iran could threaten the investment and development projects at the heart of Riyadh's economic strategy.
"For Saudi Arabia, both the current situation and a war with Iran carry serious costs," Dorbeiki said. "Its preferred route is, therefore, a diplomatic solution."
What now for Saudi Arabia after Riyadh airport attack?

Moreover, Pakistan has spent months mediating between Washington and Tehran and has important relations with both. A direct conflict would also distract Islamabad from its long-standing security concerns involving India.

Turkey is a NATO member, but Dorbeiki says direct military support for Iran against the United States is highly improbable. The fact that Ankara sent intelligence chief Ibrahim Kalin rather than its foreign or defense minister also suggests a cautious approach.
Iran pursues diplomacy while preparing for fighting
Ali Asghar Shafieian, media advisor for Iran's President Masoud Pezeshkian, also rejects the perspective that the Mecca pact representatives were trying to present Tehran with an ultimatum.
He told DW that the three countries may also have wanted to demonstrate their own growing coordination, while showing that Iran remains part of regional diplomacy.
"You cannot conclude from this meeting alone that it was an ultimatum before an attack," Shafieian said.
He also noted that Iran, just like the US and Israel, could prepare for the possibility of further conflict while maintaining negotiations.
Mediator or enforcer? Pakistan's role in the Middle East
"Just as they use the opportunity to strengthen their military and defensive capabilities, Iran does the same," he said.
Shafieian said an agreement remains possible if Iran's political standing and what Tehran describes as its national dignity are respected.
Diplomatic game continues
Analyst Dorbeiki argues that Iran is following a familiar strategy of extending negotiations while avoiding real-world commitments.
The Houthi rebels are central to Tehran's calculation.

Tehran has not publicly offered the kind of guarantees over Houthi attacks that Riyadh would want. Dorbeiki believes Iran could seek to trade influence over such the attacks for concessions such as an end to US military pressure and broader steps toward ending the war.
The only apparent outcome of the Tehran meeting is to keep talking. For Iran, that might be enough of a signal that it is still a diplomatic partner rather than an enemy.

articles.title: Mans Carpio is 'aggrieved party' in cyber libel case vs. Philip Lustre, says spokesman
articles.summary: Atty. Manases Carpio is the aggrieved party in the case against veteran journalist Philip Lustre Jr., the former"s spokesperson said on Tuesday.

blocks.text: Published October 28, 2026 10:18pm
Atty. Manases Carpio is the aggrieved party in the case against veteran journalist Philip Lustre Jr., the former’s spokesperson said on Tuesday.
Lawyer Neil Abayo, a spokesman for the husband of Vice President Sara Duterte, refuted accusations that the libel case against Lustre was an act to silence the press.

“Kung hindi siya nag post ng malicious and baseless possible libelous statement, hindi mangyayari na makakasuhan ang isang individual,” Abayon said. (If he did not post the malicious and baseless possible libelous statement, an individual will not be faced with a case.)
“Atty. Mans is actually the aggrieved party here considering it is the respondent who committed the possible criminal act,” he added.
Abayon also refuted claims that the warrant was rushed and operated, saying that the complainant had nothing to do with the implementation of a warrant, as it depended on the police.
In a Facebook post on Sunday after he posted bail, Lustre said that warrant was deliberately served on a Saturday so he could stay in jail over the weekend since he could not post bail.

“If they will insinuate wrongdoing, they must show evidence to back up their allegations of bad faith or malice on the part of the law enforcement authorities. Otherwise, that will remain as baseless allegations and could taint the reputation of men in uniform who are simply doing their job,” Abayon said.
Carpio’s spokesperson also said that Lustre should address his admission that there were “backroom moves” when it came to the posting of his bail.
Last Sunday, Lustre announced that he had posted bail by using “backroom moves”.

Lustre’s arrest came only a day after Davao City lawmaker Paolo Duterte lodged libel complaints against GMA Network journalists and executives. The two incidents lead to media groups raising concerns over press freedom.

“It was definitely a special operation against me. The intention was to have me arrested on a Saturday and stay in jail on a weekend because I might not be able to post bail for my release. There was procedure flaw in the process. That was how deep the Davao Group do their thing,” Lustre said. —Jean Mangaluz/NB, GMA News

articles.title: Egypt fines prominent editor Lina Attalah and shuts independent news outlet Mada Masr
articles.summary:
Warnings of escalating clampdown on press freedom come after Cairo court convicts Attalah of managing an unlicensed website

Lina Attalah, a prominent Egyptian journalist and the…

blocks.text: Lina Attalah, a prominent Egyptian journalist and the editor-in-chief of the news outlet Mada Masr, has been released from detention by Egypt’s authorities and had her website ordered to be shut down by a court amid an intensifying crackdown on independent media in the country.
Attalah was taken briefly into custody after a Cairo court convicted her of managing an unlicensed website, prompting fresh international concerns over press freedom in Egypt.
According to Mada Masr, Attalah was released after the news outlet had paid a fine of 3m Egyptian pounds ($53,500; £40,100), prompting statements of support from global human rights groups.

“Lina Attalah was released after we paid the said fine,” said her lawyer Hassan al-Azhari. “In the process, we discovered that she had been sentenced in absentia in 2024 to a year in prison, as well as a fine of 20,000 Egyptian pounds,” he told AFP.
Attalah’s defence team had appealed that sentence, and a new court hearing was scheduled for 11 November, Azhari added.
Attalah founded Mada Masr in 2013, after coming to international prominence in 2011 during the Arab spring. An advocate for press freedom, she has been arrested on a number of occasions.

Attalah’s detention, and the ordered closure of Mada Masr – which says it had applied for a licence to operate three years ago and had no reply from Egyptian authorities – follows the arrest of the entire six-person team at the independent factchecking platform Matsadaash, who were charged with belonging to the outlawed Muslim Brotherhood.
Attalah’s legal team suggested she had been, in effect, ambushed during a court appearance, with a judge appointing a defence lawyer for her before security personnel detained her in the courtroom.

blocks.caption: Lina Attalah holds a meeting in the Mada Masr office in 2015.  Photograph: Sabry Khaled/Sabry Khaled For The Guardian

blocks.text: The crackdown “can only mean that Egypt’s security agencies are moving from years of harassing independent media to wiping them out completely”, said Hossam Bahgat, the head of the Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR), who attended the court hearing.

“This escalation validates our fears that the arrest and continued detention of the six Matsadaash journalists would signal a crackdown of unprecedented magnitude,” said Bahgat. “It risks fully eviscerating the narrow margin of press freedoms that have been carefully maintained in Egypt over the past decade, albeit amid great personal sacrifice – a margin that had allowed the continued operation of a handful of news outlets and human rights organisations despite frequent harassment, including through legal avenues.”

According to EIPR, the recent moves against independent media follow an increasing frequency of statements from the Egyptian president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, since August claiming a conspiracy to destabilise the country. He has said he intended to remain in power until 2030 to protect Egypt from “traitors, criminals, and saboteurs”.

Reporters Without Borders said the court’s decision was “outrageous” and “shameful”, urging authorities to release Attalah “at once”. The Committee to Protect Journalists (CPJ) also condemned the verdict. Amnesty International said the verdict represented “a crushing blow to press freedom”.

Egypt is among the top jailers of journalists globally, with 25 currently behind bars, according to the CPJ. Attalah’s lawyers took steps to challenge the ruling, with a hearing in a retrial of the case scheduled for 11 November.
Underlining concerns over the crackdown, Pen International issued a statement with several dozen civil society organisations condemning the moves.

“Though this is the sixth case brought against Mada Masr in six years, this is the first time that a case of this nature has been referred to trial,” the writers’ association said. “For years, Egyptian authorities have leveraged their repressive and restrictive tactics against independent media outlets to harass journalists, restrict their operations and chill freedom of expression. To escalate to the step of referral to trial must be read as a clear intent to entirely shutter the independent media space, and to permanently close what remains.”

articles.title: Cruise billed as floating home suspends global voyage over fuel costs, stranding passengers
articles.summary: A U.S. cruise ship on an around-the-world voyage that touted its cabins as floating homes suspended its three-year voyage in Cambodia due to fuel costs, forcing hundreds of passengers to disembark.

image.caption: U.S. cruise ship the MV Odyssey docks at the Sihanoukville Autonomous Port in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, on Wednesday. (Heng Sinith/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World
A U.S. cruise ship on an around-the-world voyage that touted its cabins as floating homes suspended its three-year voyage in Cambodia due to fuel costs, forcing hundreds of passengers to disembark.
The MV Odyssey is currently docked in Cambodia

The MV Odyssey set sail two years ago on a voyage to the seven continents marketed as combining long-term living at sea with global travel. Its operator had offered to "make the Odyssey your permanent home," with the purchase price of a suite for the lifetime of the vessel starting around $230,000 US, or about $323,000 Cdn.
For now, it is docked at the Cambodian port of Sihanoukville on the Gulf of Thailand, with no certain departure date.
The ship has been carrying 203 passengers, mostly Americans, along with 156 crew members, according to Cambodian officials. It has a 650-passenger capacity.

Its Florida-based operator, Villa Vie Residences, said monthly fuel expenses per cabin that historically averaged $2,527 Cdn have reached an estimated $8,425 to $11,234 in parts of Asia due to the war in Iran.
The company said it sought to reduce fuel consumption by slowing the itinerary and spending more time in port, but was unable to offset the surging costs.
The Odyssey, an around-the-world voyage that touted its cabins as floating homes, seen here in Japan in a press kit photo, has suspended its three-year voyage. (Odyssey/The Associated Press)
Traffic has been curtailed in the Strait of Hormuz since the Iran war began, squeezing supplies of all kinds of petroleum-based fuels, especially in Southeast Asia, and sharply increasing prices.
"We have been unable to continue carrying the resulting operating losses," Villa Vie Residences said in a statement issued Tuesday.

items: Oil trading in triple digits, but Canadian crude selling at steeper discount
The price of diesel is skyrocketing. Here's why Canadians may soon feel it at the grocery store

blocks.text: "Passing the full increase on to residents is not a realistic solution. Our focus now is on supporting residents, crew, and employees," the company said, while it tries to restructure.
"The company is working with residents to co-ordinate disembarkation and identify temporary living arrangements," it said.
Those on the ship had hoped to sail for years to come

Passengers, however, said they received no support and had to make their own arrangements after being given seven hours notice on Tuesday to disembark. Some were devastated and expressed hope a new company could rescue the venture so life at sea can continue.
Paul and Lynn Montoya, a retired couple from Wyoming, said they bought a window cabin and had expected to sail for years. They boarded the ship 17 months ago in Panama.

Passengers from the MV Odyssey, Paul Montoya, left, and his wife, Lynn Motoya, stand for an interview at the Independence Hotel in Sihanoukville, Cambodia, on Wednesday. (Heng Sinith/The Associated Press)

Paul praised the concept of residential cruising but said the shipowner lacked the expertise to make the business financially sustainable. While rising fuel costs had been cited publicly as the reason for the suspension, he said the company had already been struggling. Changes to itinerary, unreliable internet access and declining food quality had pushed many residents to leave the ship in recent months, he said.

Lynn said residents were repeatedly asked to contribute additional money for fuel and other expenses, including a fresh call to raise funds for fuel to get out of Cambodia. She said the crew members were also not paid.

"We were tired of every two to four weeks being asked for money for fuel, money for everything," she said. "We had hopes but they just kept sinking further and further into the hole through mismanagement."
The company could not immediately be contacted for comment.
For some, the venture was a worth risk taking
Yet for some, even the financial and logistical turmoil couldn't outweigh the extraordinary experience of travelling the world and living at sea.

Carol Larson, 69, and her sister Crystal Lavering, 72, occupied separate cabins aboard the ship for 18 months. The siblings, from California, described the suspension as heartbreaking, and hoped the cruise would be resuscitated.
"I hope there is a movement for the residents to buy the ship and I am hoping that goes through because it's a dream to live on the ship and I don’t want it to end," Larson said.
Lavering said her health improved during her time on the ship, and that she didn’t need to use a cane to walk anymore. "You come to this ship to live … it's just sad that it’s all over."

Larson bought her cabin for $168,000 Cdn, paid in installments, in addition to monthly maintenance fees, under a plan that had promised the possibility of living aboard for up to 15 years. She said she blamed U.S. President Donald Trump for the ship's woes as fuel costs spiked due to the Iran war, in addition to poor management. But she said she didn't regret her investment.

"Because it was a startup company, I believe that it was a risk. From the very first day, I said to myself that if it lasts a year, I can walk away and feel like I got my money's worth," she said. "I still feel that way. I feel blessed to have been part of the experiment of residential cruising."

Sisters Carol Larson, 69, left, and Crystal Lavering, both passengers from U.S. cruise ship MV Odyssey, speak outside the Independence Hotel in Sihanoukville on Wednesday. (Heng Sinith/The Associated Press)
The cruise began in Northern Ireland in 2024

The ship arrived in Sihanoukville last Friday and was scheduled to depart Wednesday, according to a statement from Long Dimanche, the deputy governor of Preah Sihanouk province. He said it was now expected to refuel and depart Cambodia on Saturday, but the ship's operator has not yet publicly confirmed any date.

Built in 1993 and operated under different names by several cruise lines over the years before being becalmed by the coronavirus pandemic in 2020, the Odyssey was bought by Villa Vie Residences in 2023.
Its current cruise, originally intended to last 3½ years, began in October 2024 in Belfast, where the ship had been refitted. A second cruise had been tentatively scheduled to end in August 2030.

articles.summary: NSW government imposes water restrictions after Menindee water volumes fall below 2021 levels
articles.byline: Lisa Cox Environment and climate correspondent

blocks.text: Water levels at Menindee Lakes in western New South Wales have fallen to their lowest point in five years, prompting the state government to impose upstream water use restrictions as experts warn of potential mass fish deaths over summer.
Combined storage at Menindee Lakes fell below 480 gigalitres earlier this month, the first time since 2021.
In the upper Menindee Lakes, water volumes have dropped below 250GL, a level that triggers temporary state water restrictions across parts of the northern Murray-Darling basin.
The restrictions limit access for some irrigators and are intended to preserve water for critical human needs and the environment.

It follows periods of low rainfall in the catchment throughout the past 12 months, with experts warning of a growing risk of summer fish kills unless flows down to Menindee Lakes via the Darling-Baaka River improve.
Menindee was the site of catastrophic fish kills in 2018, 2019 and 2023, which saw millions of dead fish wash up along stretches of the Darling-Baaka.

“Government officials are predicting with a level of certainty that unless there’s more water flowing into the Baaka-Darling River that there will be fish kills at Menindee this summer,” said Prof Jamie Pittock of the Australian National University and the Wentworth Group of Concerned Scientists.
“We need a major rainfall event to happen and for the state governments to prevent irrigators from pumping out the first flush of water.”
Graeme McCrabb, who was one of the first Menindee residents to raise the alarm about the 2018-19 disasters, said the combined Menindee Lakes had reached “drought reserve volumes”.
He said this effectively meant conservation of water “at all costs”. McCrabb said he was hopeful that recent rainfall in Queensland may result in some replenishment of the Menindee system.
“There are some small inflows coming across the Queensland border now which probably give us some hope for the summer. But we would need more on top of that,” he said.
“If we don’t get inflows, the risk [of fish kills] would be very high in January or February.”
He said a milder summer would also lower the risk.
after newsletter promotion
“I’m worried about fish kills to be honest,” McCrabb said.
“It’s a tough time or sad time when the water starts to get that real green algal look.”
Days after winning the 2023 state election, the premier, Chris Minns, and senior state ministers visited Menindee and committed to an investigation of the mass fish kills.

An expert panel was established under the northern basin connectivity program, which recommended limiting upstream overextraction during dry periods, to help maintain flows in tributaries into the Darling-Baaka River to Menindee Lakes. This was to try to reduce the risk of catastrophes such as fish kills and large-scale drying.
The panel delivered its final report two years ago but the state government is yet to implement it.
McCrabb said he was disappointed the government had not followed through on the recommendations of the connectivity panel.
“Since the fish kills, government agencies have made no policy changes to improve water quality outcomes,” he said.
Comment has been sought from the NSW water minister, Rose Jackson.

articles.title: Gen Z protests in Germany: Is France-style violence looming?
articles.summary: Young people in Germany will take to the streets this weekend to demand education and action on climate change. Politicians warn that the protests could become violent, as in France, but the…

image.caption: Young people have already been protesting against the reintroduction of military serviceImage: Snowfield Photography/picture alliance

blocks.text: As politicians in Germany look ahead to the coming weekend, many fear that cities across the country could witness the kind of violent unrest that recently shook France. An initiative known as "Gen Z regelt" ("Gen Z sorts it") has launched a social media campaign calling for demonstrations in 23 cities nationwide.

"Gen Z" broadly refers to the generation born between 1995 and 2010. Many feel that their parents' generation has done too little to combat climate change and has allowed the gap between rich and poor to widen ever further. At the same time, they are concerned about their educational prospects and future opportunities in Western societies.
CDU: 'We must prevent scenes like those in France at all costs'

In France, what began as largely peaceful protests recently spiraled into serious unrest. Cars were set alight in several towns, while in Limoges the town hall was torched. In Lille, Lyon, and Toulouse and elsewhere, police deployed tear gas, leading to numerous arrests.
Many politicians, particularly within Chancellor Friedrich Merz's center-right Christian Democratic Union (CDU), are warning of similar scenes this coming weekend.
Alexander Throm, the CDU parliamentary group's domestic spokesperson, told the daily Handelsblatt newspaper: "Scenes like those in France must be prevented at all costs."
France protests continue despite police crackdown
Concerns over internationally coordinated far-left extremists
In Throm's view, far-left groups and criminals from immigrant communities could "hijack" the demonstrations. "An ominous alliance is emerging, particularly in Berlin," he warned.

Marc Henrichmann, also of the CDU, chair of the Bundestag's parliamentary oversight panel for the intelligence services, also expressed concern: "The far-left extremist scene is internationally connected and coordinated." He said that violent far-left activists now even cross national borders to engage in looting and acts of violence elsewhere.

But Sebastian Koos, sociologist at the University of Konstanz whose research focuses on youth and protest movements, told DW that he does not expect Germany to experience unrest on a scale comparable to that seen in France, even though events in the neighboring country helped spark the protests now being planned across Germany.
Koos: 'Not driven by anger as in France'

Koos sees key differences between young people in the two countries. "Unlike in France, these protests are not driven by the same level of anger," he said. "They have been planned, officially registered and carefully organized. The website, in particular, places strong emphasis on peaceful protest and repeatedly stresses a non-violent approach."

At the same time, the sociologist does not rule out the possibility that extremist groups could exploit the authorized demonstrations to stir up unrest: "It is certainly very important for the police and public authorities to be well prepared."

Quentin Gärtner, 19, studies biotechnology in Heidelberg and served until November of last year as secretary-general of the Federal Student Conference, which represents around 7.5 million school students in Germany.

"What unites us is that we have run out of patience with the education system. Many young people are deeply frustrated," he told DW. "The performance of German school students continues to decline, teaching positions are constantly being cut, and in many cases school buildings have seen little or no meaningful investment for years."

blocks.caption: Alexander Throm of the CDU has warned against far-left extremist violenceImage: Christoph Soeder/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Greens express understanding for the protests

For Gärtner, the discontent reflects a broader problem with parliamentary democracy in Germany and many other Western countries: "Politicians want to win elections. They focus on the groups that matter most to them electorally rather than on the future and the long-term sustainability of their policies," he said. "And in our aging societies, older people and the baby boomer generation are the groups that carry the most political weight."

Opposition parties in Germany have also voiced understanding for the concerns of younger people. Speaking to Germany's public broadcaster ZDF, Green Party co-leader Felix Banaszak said: "The intergenerational contract is no longer working. Older generations have driven the climate into a dead end."

He argued that the social welfare system was also reaching its limits and that rents had become unaffordable. According to Banaszak, the only thing the state seems to offer young people are the letters sent to 18-year-olds asking them to consider joining the military. Germany is currently desperate to expand the Bundeswehr and is considering reintroducing national service.

By Tuesday, around 134,000 people had registered on the "Gen Z regelt" website to take part in the protests planned for the coming Saturday. With several days still to go before the demonstrations, that number could rise further.
This article was translated from German.

articles.title: At least 64 people killed in Spain as 2 high-speed trains collide
articles.summary: 'We heard a massive roar, a truly enormous thud that went on for 10 seconds, as if the train were about to derail. Through the right-hand window, we could see a wrecked train,' says a passenger…

blocks.text: COLLISION. Emergency teams work at the scene of a collision involving two high-speed trains near Urda station in Toledo province, Spain, on October 28, 2026.
Burak Akbulut/Anadolu

'We heard a massive roar, a truly enormous thud that went on for 10 seconds, as if the train were about to derail. Through the right-hand window, we could see a wrecked train,' says a passenger traveling with several colleagues in the rear car of one of the trains

URDA, Spain – Rescue workers in Spain on Wednesday, October 28, were scouring the wreckage for more bodies at the crash scene where at least 64 people were killed when two high-speed trains collided, in the second deadly railway accident in the country this year.

Evacuated passengers streamed along a road near the scene, some splattered with blood or with their wounds bandaged, others wheeling suitcases and being given water by volunteers who said it had been donated from neighboring towns.

Hundreds of ambulances, funeral home vans and helicopters were parked next to a train with several carriages sitting on an elevated section of track while twisted metal, broken panels and wreckage could be seen strewn across an embankment beneath the line where at least three carriages had plunged.
Miguel, a passenger traveling with several colleagues in the rear car of one of the trains, described to COPE radio the moment of the accident.
“We heard a massive roar, a truly enormous thud that went on for 10 seconds, as if the train were about to derail. Through the right-hand window, we could see a wrecked train,” he said.
A person briefed on the disaster said a train operated by private consortium Iryo stopped near Toledo on orders from infrastructure manager ADIF due to a signal fault.
A train operated by Renfe then struck the stationary train at high speed, causing several carriages of both trains to derail, the person said.
Renfe said in a statement that after a being authorized to continue its journey, its train had crashed into the Iryo train that had remained stationary “for reasons we don’t know.”

“The Renfe train continued on its way as instructed, and a collision occurred. The exact sequence of events, the traffic conditions and the circumstances of the impact will have to be established by the investigation,” Renfe said.
There was no immediate response to a Reuters request for comment from Iryo or Adif. – Rappler.com

articles.title: EXPLAINER: What is the Free Funeral Services Act?
articles.summary: On September 28, 2025, Republic Act No. 12309, or the “Free Funeral Services Act,” lapsed into law after 30 days without President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.'s signature. This law institutionalized the…

blocks.text: Did you know that the government is mandated by law to provide free funeral services to poor Filipinos who cannot afford a decent burial for their loved ones?
On September 28, 2025, Republic Act No. 12309, or the “Free Funeral Services Act,” lapsed into law after remaining unacted upon for 30 days without the signature of President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.
This law institutionalized the Department of Social Welfare and Development’s (DSWD) funeral assistance initiative through its Aid to Individuals in Crisis Situation (AICS) program.

Under RA 12309, free funeral services must be extended to families in crisis situations, as determined by the DSWD, including indigent families, those affected by calamities or disasters, and individuals facing emergency circumstances that prevent them from affording dignified burial services.
How does the law grant its beneficiaries a decent funeral?
Beneficiary
According to the Free Funeral Services Act, the service is provided to “poor families per death of a family member.”
The law defines “poor families” as those whose income falls below the poverty threshold as defined by the Department of Economy, Planning, and Development.
This classification also includes those unable to meet basic needs, such as food, health, education, and housing, as defined under the Social Reform and Poverty Alleviation Act.

For 2025, the poverty threshold was set at a national average of P14,634 per month, up from P13,873 in 2023. Meaning, this figure represents the minimum income required for a family to meet its basic food and non-food needs.
Under this 2025 threshold, a family whose monthly income falls below the threshold is considered poor.
How to avail the assistance?
Free funeral services may be obtained from accredited funeral establishments nationwide that offer a standardized indigent funeral package.
“Free funeral services shall be provided to poor families per death of a family member by accredited funeral establishment anywhere in the country,” the law said.

Funeral establishments refer to licensed businesses that provide services such as funeral parlors, chapels, and similar facilities used for preparing, transporting, storing, and caring for the deceased prior to burial or cremation.
The free funeral package covers the preparation of funeral documents, embalming, burial, cremation, inurnment, transportation, and the provision of a casket or urn.
To avail of the indigent funeral package, under the law, the bereaved family or an authorized representative must present the following requirements:

items: Valid identification card of the claimant or beneficiary;
Death certificate issued by the hospital or city/municipal health office, or certification from the tribal chieftain;
Funeral contract signed by the representative of the deceased's family, the funeral establishment, and an authorized DSWD personnel; and
Social care study prepared by any registered social worker

blocks.text: At present, the DSWD also requires additional documents depending on the specific services requested. Further details are available through the DSWD AICS Funeral Assistance Portal.
Upon the approval of the DSWD Regional Director, the agency pays the funeral establishment for the indigent package rendered to the beneficiary.

“The payment will be based on the stipulations of the signed contract between the representative of the deceased's family, the funeral establishment, and the authorized DSWD personnel,” the law notes.
Penalties for violations
Funeral establishments that refuse to provide free funeral services face a maximum fine of P400,000, alongside the revocation of their operating license.
Meanwhile, individuals who fraudulently avail of the free funeral service face up to six months of imprisonment and a maximum fine of P500,000.

Data from the DSWD show that from 2014 to September 2025, the agency extended burial assistance to families of 1,439,160 individuals, releasing a total of P10.9 million through the AICS program. —LDF, GMA News

articles.title: Moody skies, ocean views and local talent: B.C. shines in new Crave series Yaga
articles.summary: Producers say B.C. was the perfect spot to film the new series Yaga, a supernatural mystery inspired by Slavic folklore around Baba Yaga. The series has been trending high on Crave since it premiered…

image.caption: Vancouver Island's coastline, as seen here, is a big part of the new Crave series Yaga. (Christopher Lawrence/Crave)

blocks.text: British Columbia

Producers say B.C. was the perfect spot to film the new series Yaga, a supernatural mystery inspired by Slavic folklore around Baba Yaga. The series has been trending high on Crave since it premiered on Oct. 23.
Supernatural mystery series inspired by legend of Baba Yaga trending on Crave since it premiered Oct. 23
It's a quiet autumn day on southern Vancouver Island. Fog settles in among the trees and the grey sky reflects off the water. It feels, to some degree, eerie.

That's what made it the perfect spot to film the new series Yaga — a new supernatural mystery inspired by Slavic folklore around Baba Yaga — that has been trending on Crave since it premiered on Oct. 23.
Rugged coastlines and dense forests feature prominently in the series, produced by Blink49 Studios and Vancouver-based company Front Street Pictures.
Not only was the setting ideal, but the pool of local actors and crew made B.C. an attractive option for producers.

items: More stories from Vancouver Island

blocks.text: "British Columbia has an extraordinary depth of talent, both in front of and behind the camera, and a production infrastructure that makes it possible to bring ambitious stories to life," Pancho Mansfield, Blink49 Studios' president of global scripted television, said in a statement.

"To now see Yaga at No. 1 on Crave is incredibly rewarding. It speaks to the work of our cast and crew and creative partners, and is a great reminder of what B.C. filmmaking can deliver when local talent and compelling storytelling come together."
Hudson Williams' new show Yaga is here
Yaga follows a private detective investigating the disappearance of local heir, Henry Park, played by B.C. actor Hudson Williams of Heated Rivalry fame.

items: From The Matrix to Yaga, Carrie-Anne Moss still believes rejection can open the right door

blocks.text: While Williams, who has ties to Kamloops, Kelowna and New Westminster, is certainly a local talent that will draw viewers, the series also stars Burnaby-born Carrie-Anne Moss, who some may recognize from her roles in The Matrix films and Chocolat, or from several Marvel Cinematic Universe series including Jessica Jones and Daredevil.
B.C.-born actors Hudson Williams and Carrie-Anne Moss star in the new Crave series Yaga. (Christopher Lawrence/Crave)

Vancouver's Emilija Baranac, who played Midge in Riverdale, also makes an appearance, as well as Ezra Franky, an Ulkatcho First Nation actor and musician whose character, Pam Russell, piques the interest of investigators given her history with the missing man.

"Pam is very independent," Franky told CBC's On The Coast. "She's an athlete, she's a student … she is also Henry Park's ex-girlfriend, but I like to say that's the least interesting thing about her."
British Columbia, and particularly Vancouver Island, was the perfect place to shoot the series, she said.
B.C.'s coast features prominently in the new Crave series Yaga. (Christopher Lawrence/Crave)

"There's a moodiness to the Island that sets the tone in Yaga really well. And the small-town energy in Victoria just fuels the mystery: everyone knows everyone's business and you don't know who to trust.
"It's so beautiful filming in B.C.. We have city, country, mountains, ocean, or really whatever environment your story calls for, right at our fingertips."
Ulkatcho First Nation actor and musician Ezra Franky is one of the stars of Yaga. (Christopher Lawrence/Crave)

items: Yaga star Ezra Franky loves reading complex ‘witchy’ women

blocks.text: Castmate Williams got himself in hot — or maybe lukewarm — water with some locals in March when he said at Paris Fashion Week that the city was "dead as f–k," and then again in October when he made similar comments about the city's "hot spots" during an interview with etalk.
"A lot of hot spots of old people on the little scooters, people retiring, like, that's Victoria. Hot spots for what? Like retirement homes and fricking bingo? I'm sorry Victoria."
Franky said his comments were funny, and very honest.
"It's Canada," she said with a laugh. "If you go and find the fun, the fun will find you."
She enjoyed working with Williams, who she described as a "very good actor and a great scene partner."
"He is such a joy to work with," Franky said. "He always made the situation very comfortable and safe to explore the character."
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Courtney Dickson is a journalist with CBC News based in Vancouver, covering stories throughout B.C. She has previously worked for CBC in Kamloops and Toronto. She has won Radio Television Digital News Association awards locally and nationally, and in 2022, won a Webster Award.
With files from On The Coast
