blocks.text: October 28, 2026
Situation barely moves as more than 80% of vote counted

Partial results published by the Central Elections Committee and reported by the Times of Israel newspaper showed the bloc led by Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on 54 seats, with 84.5% of votes counted.
The opposition bloc under Gadi Eisenkot of the centrist Yashar party was on 49 seats.
Neither bloc is set to received the 61 seats need for a majority in the 120-seat Knesset, making some form of coalition likely.
The Arab-led parties — the Joint List and the United Arab List, commonly known under its Hebrew name of Ra’am — have dropped to 17 seats.
The numbers are still likely to change, particularly after a record number of absentee votes are counted.
The full tally of those will possibly not be confirmed until Friday, according to the newspaper.

articles.title: Australia must recruit hundreds more to crew Aukus submarines, retired admiral warns
articles.summary:
As USS Colorado showcases the program in Perth, Peter Briggs says personnel is just one of the ‘huge issues’ it faces

  • Get our

blocks.text: Australia faces an uphill battle to recruit and train enough naval personnel to serve on submarines planned for the future fleet of nuclear-powered vessels under the controversial $368bn Aukus deal, a retired admiral has warned.

As the Virginia-class submarine USS Colorado arrived at HMAS Stirling south of Perth on Tuesday for a month of routine maintenance and to help build Australian expertise, retired admiral Peter Briggs said more people needed to be enrolled in the navy’s submarine program.

As part of a $368bn trilateral defence deal, Australia will acquire between three and five Virginia-class, nuclear-powered submarines from the United States to replace its five diesel-electric Collins-class vessels, which are becoming obsolete.
The new submarines are much bigger and require up to 134 crew – almost three times the number needed for the Collins class.
The Royal Australian Navy says it has 230 personnel in various stage of the US nuclear-powered submarine training pipeline.

blocks.caption: Captain Justin Reeves talks to the media on USS Colorado at HMAS Stirling in Perth. Photograph: Richard Wainwright/AAP

blocks.text: “Of these, approximately 145 have completed US Naval nuclear power training and are now building experience training on US Navy SSNs [a hull classification for nuclear-powered submarines],” a navy spokesperson said.
“By 2030, we expect to have 400 Royal Australian Navy officers and sailors trained and ready to serve.”
But Briggs urged a more intensive recruitment plan to crew the bigger boats.
“We have got to triple the size of the submarine arm and we’ve got to train them in nuclear skills,” he said.
“You are heading toward needing a submarine arm of 3,000, that’s the hill you have to climb.”
Approximately 850 submariners are qualified to operate Collins-class vessels.
The Virginia-class boats are intended to bridge the transition from the Collins-class fleet to the future SSN-AUKUS submarine, an even bigger design being developed by Australia and the UK.

blocks.caption: Crew members on the USS Colorado. Photograph: Richard Wainwright/AAP

blocks.text: “The personnel side is a huge issue, but it’s not the only one,” Briggs said.
The former submariner argued that maintaining two different submarine types would add complexity to training, logistics, maintenance and spare-parts arrangements.
The Australian government did not respond to questions about recruitment targets and whether a workforce development program was on track.
Recruitment is further complicated by the need for more than a dozen different trades, from radio and sonar operators to cooks and electricians.

After spending the next month is Perth, the USS Colorado will return to the city’s waters again in late 2027 as part of the Submarine Rotational Force-West program which is designed to help Australia build the skills and infrastructure to operate its own nuclear fleet.
From 2027, the program will see up to four US and one UK nuclear-powered submarine rotate through HMAS Stirling.

Paul Johnson, HMAS Stirling fleet base west commodore, said the USS Colorado maintenance period would be used to “practise and test our procedures across a range of nuclear-related operational scenarios”.
Officials stressed that no radiological material would be transferred during the maintenance period and that nuclear-related exercises would be simulated.
Late last year, Senate estimates heard that US submarines carrying nuclear weapons could rotate through Australian ports despite a non-proliferation commitment.
USS Colorado captain, Justin Reeves, said the US government would not “confirm or deny the presence of nuclear weapons on specific platforms”.
Colorado was built in 2018 and arrived this week carrying conventional weapons, including four torpedoes and four “payload tubes” that can be used to house and launch weapons.

It took two weeks to travel to Perth from Pearl Harbor in Hawaii with 160 men and no women aboard. A sign labelled “Berth Rules”, taped to the wall near the submarine’s entryway, listed “Don’t be stinky” as the crew’s top priority once they reach port.

blocks.caption: Sleeping quarters on the USS Colorado. Photograph: Richard Wainwright/AAP

blocks.text: The demands of living and working in confined spaces for extended periods presents another recruitment challenge for officials.
Sleeping arrangements can involve bunks stacked three high, while “hot racking” allows three sailors to share two beds by rotating their sleeping schedules around watch duties.
In some circumstances, and when accommodation is limited, sailors may sleep in torpedo rooms.
Reeves said the vessel is “built for combat, not for comfort”.
Nuclear submarines don’t need to refuel, meaning their range is effectively infinite. “The limits of its endurance are really food and toilet paper, and that’s several months’ worth,” Reeves said.
“Being nuclear powered is a massive advantage.”

articles.title: Comelec to resume voter registration for 2028 polls on Nov. 10
articles.summary: The Commission on Elections (Comelec) will resume voter registration on November 10 ahead of the 2028 national and local elections, Chairperson George Garcia said on Wednesday.

blocks.text: Published October 28, 2026 8:40pm
The Commission on Elections (Comelec) will resume voter registration on November 10 ahead of the 2028 national and local elections, Chairperson George Garcia said on Wednesday.
Garcia said the registration period would run until July 30, 2027.

“Sa mga kababayan natin na gustong magparehistro dahil hindi sila rehistrado, magpa-revive ng registration, magpa-transfer ng kanilang registration, o kaya naman magpa-reactivate ng kanilang registration, o magpabago sa kahit anong datos doon, gawin nyo po 'yan mula November 10 at ito po ay tatagal hanggang sa next year, as much as possible July 30,” Garcia told reporters.

(Those who wish to register as voters, reactivate or transfer their registration, or update any information in their records may do so starting November 10. The registration period is expected to last until July 30 next year.)
The poll body earlier said around 74 million Filipinos are expected to be eligible to vote in the May 2028 national and local elections.
Comelec also projected that an additional one million voters would be eligible to vote in the November 2028 Barangay and Sangguniang Kabataan Elections (BSKE). — Vince Angelo Ferreras/VBL, GMA News

articles.title: Alex Eala advances to Toray Pan Pacific quarterfinals after besting Talia Gibson
articles.summary: Eala is now set to face Russian player Diana Shnaider, who previously defeated her in the second round of the Ningbo Open in China

blocks.text: FILIPINA TENNIS STAR. Alex Eala at the Toray Pan Pacific Open in Tokyo, Japan.
Toray Pan Pacific Open website
Eala is now set to face Russian player Diana Shnaider, who previously defeated her in the second round of the Ningbo Open in China
MANILA, Philippines – Alex Eala pulls off a triumphant win over Australia’s Talia Gibson, 4-6, 6-2, 6-0, in the Toray Pan Pacific Open round of 16 match in Tokyo, Japan, on Wednesday, October 28.

Eala had gotten off to a rough start after losing the first set to her World No. 38 opponent, 4-6. It had been smooth sailing in the succeeding sets, 6-2, 6-0, as she was able to contain Gibson by a large margin.
“I think really staying in the match [and] never giving up,” Eala explained in a post-game interview when asked what the key to her victory was.
“The first set was difficult, and I had my chances, so I knew that if I kept my concentration I would have more chances.”

This is not the first time the two players went head-to-head with each other. Eala and Gibson had previously played against each other at the IXXVII Open Generali Ciudad de Palma del Rio round of 16 in June 2023, and then in the ITF W25 Aldershot GB Pro Series round of 16 in August 2023. The Filipina won both matches.
The Filipina tennis star will now face Diana Shnaider of Russia in the quarterfinals on Friday, October 30.
Just before Eala made her Toray Pan Pacific Open debut, she had suffered a second-round exit at the hands of Shnaider at the Ningbo Open in China on October 22. – Rappler.com

articles.title: Toxics watchdog urges parents to avoid unauthorized squishy toys for safety
articles.summary: A Toxics Watchdog has issued a reminder to parents and consumers on Tuesday to refrain from purchasing unauthorized squishy toys to reduce the risk of toxic exposure among children.

blocks.text: Published October 28, 2026 8:34pm
A Toxics watchdog has issued a reminder to parents and consumers on Tuesday to refrain from purchasing unauthorized squishy toys to reduce the risk of toxic exposure among children.

BAN Toxics took note of the public health advisories posted by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA) against the purchase and use of unauthorized Toy and Childcare Article (TCCA) products, ‘Squishy Delicious’ toys.

"The FDA advisory follows an earlier consumer alert by BAN Toxics over food-like squeezy dumpling toys that have gained popularity online. Resembling steamed buns, these products continue to be sold in retail stores and through online shopping platforms," the group said.
The toys are available in different sizes and colors, some contain glitter, and cost from P80 to P200 in retail stories and between P60 to P150 through online shopping sites.
It can be recalled that the FDA issued its advisories in September on the purchase and use of the unauthorized squishy toys Squishy Delicious Blue and Squishy Delicious Green.
The purchase and use of the toys are unauthorized because these have not been issued the required Certificate of Product Notification (CPN).
Potential hazards
"Since the toys have not undergone the FDA notification process, the agency cannot assure their quality and safety," the group said.

"Potential hazards may arise from ingredients that are not permitted in toy and childcare article products. The use of substandard and possibly adulterated products may pose health risks, including endocrine disruption and reproductive or developmental effects, as well as injuries, choking, or suffocation due to small or broken parts," they added.
There were reported product recalls in the UK and US, for squishy dumpling toys "due to excessive concentrations of benzene, posing a serious chemical risk to children’s health and safety."

According to the UK Office for Product Safety and Standards, “The product presents a serious chemical risk because the outer layer contains an excessive concentration of benzene (20 mg/kg). If inhaled, benzene can cause irritation to the eyes, nose, and throat. Exposure to large amounts may also cause a burning sensation in the digestive tract and skin irritation.”
Health effects

Ban Toxics cited a statement issued by the World Health Organization (WHO) that “Human exposure to benzene has been associated with a range of acute and long-term adverse health effects and diseases, including cancer and haematological effects. Exposure can occur occupationally, in the general environment, and in the home as a result of the widespread use of benzene-containing petroleum products.”

The Department of Environment and Natural Resources (DENR) issued Administrative Order No. 2026-29 on the Chemical Control Order for Benzene, which stated that this chemical should not be used in toys and other children’s products.

“We laud the FDA and the DENR for their regulatory actions against unauthorized toys that may contain chemicals that pose risks to a child’s health and development,” said Thony Dizon, Advocacy and Campaign Officer of BAN Toxics.
“It is high time for government agencies to enforce the law and immediately recall and remove the products from the market.”

Ban Toxics also cited Republic Act No. 10620 or the Toy and Game Safety Labeling Act of 2013, which provides that all toys and games, whether locally manufactured or imported, distributed, donated, or sold in the Philippines, must comply with the applicable safety labeling and manufacturer’s marking requirements under the Philippine National Standards (PNS) for toy safety. — BAP, GMA News

articles.title: Bank of Canada governor says rate hike to 2.5% was needed in face of persistent inflation

image.caption: Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem during a news conference in Ottawa on Wednesday. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)

blocks.text: Why now? Tiff Macklem asked what central bank aims to accomplish with rate hike

Bank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem, when asked what the central bank was trying to accomplish with its first rate hike since 2023, acknowledged the complexity of the global economic situation, particularly around increased energy prices. But he said the policy rate — even with the increase — is 'low enough that it's not restraining growth' but will help get inflation back to target 'more quickly.'
The Latest

items: The Bank of Canada has raised its benchmark interest rate a quarter-point to 2.5 per cent.

The bank said the increase is needed to reduce the risk of higher energy prices fuelling broader inflation. Canada's annual inflation rate rose to 3.1 per cent in September, largely driven by surging energy prices due to the war in the Middle East.
The bank's governor Tiff Macklem had kept the interest rate at 2.25 for seven consecutive meetings. Today's hike marks the bank's first rate change in a year and the first rate hike since 2023.
Macklem faces a difficult balancing act: raising interest rates could help slow inflation, but could also weaken growth in an already struggling labour market.
The Bank of Canada's next rate decision is scheduled for Dec. 9.

October 28Takeaways from today's Bank of Canada rate hikeBank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem during a news conference in Ottawa on Wednesday. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)We're wrapping up our live coverage of the Bank of Canada's interest rate announcement. Here are some of the key takeaways from today's decision.The central bank raised its benchmark interest rate by a quarter-point to 2.5 per cent, marking its first change after seven consecutive holds and its first increase since July 2023.Governor Tiff Macklem said the hike was "needed to reduce the risk that elevated energy prices could spill over and become generalized inflation."As the war in the Middle East has kept oil prices high, the bank expects inflation to reach roughly 3.5 per cent by the end of 2026 and remain at or above three per cent for much of next year.The bank's outlook for economic growth has improved slightly, though, with the Canadian economy expected to grow two per cent next year. He also said the Canadian economy showed signs of resilience through the middle of 2026, growing 3.3 per cent in the second quarter.Still, Macklem noted that uncertainty surrounding U.S. tariffs and the conflict in the Middle East continues to weigh on the economy.Today's hike also means higher borrowing costs for Canadians, including prospective homebuyers. Deputy governor Carolyn Rogers said the housing market is already struggling, particularly in Ontario and British Columbia, and that the rate increase will add to those pressures.The bank hasn't ruled out more hikes, but Macklem stressed that future decisions will be made "one meeting at a time.""There could be a need to increase the policy rate further, but given uncertainties, Governing Council agreed to proceed carefully," the bank said.

Hike will weigh on variable mortgage holders: brokerAbby HughesHouses are pictured in Vancouver, B.C., on April 4, 2024. (Ben Nelms/CBC)Mortgage broker Marcus Tzaferis says today's rate decision might not do much to weigh on the housing market by keeping new buyers on the sidelines, because so many Canadians are already choosing not to buy.But it will weigh on mortgage holders.Those with variable rates will feel it the most. On a $500,000 mortgage, a rate hike of 25 basis points would add about $70 per month on average to a holder's monthly payments.While that might not seem like much, Tzaferis says Canadians are already struggling with the high cost of living, pointing to a rise in insolvencies as a sign consumers are having a tough time."To a consumer that's already stretched, these 25 basis point incremental increases are going to have an impact," Tzaferis said.For variable rate holders who are thinking about the impact that rising rates could have and want more predictability, Tzaferis says "now is the time" to try and lock in a fixed mortgage.And for those who will need to renegotiate a mortgage within the next year, Tzaferis says they have the option to lock in a fixed rate further in advance, "almost like an insurance policy for themselves," which could make sense for some.

Bank could've held off on raising rates, says economistAbby HughesPedro Antunes is the chief economist at Signal 49, an independent research firm. He says the bank could have held off longer before raising rates, but understands why the governing council would have wanted to guard against inflation. (CBC)Pedro Antunes, chief economist at independent research firm Signal 49, says he thinks the bank could have held off longer before raising rates.Looking at last month's inflation numbers, Antunes says inflation from oil still hasn't started spilling over into the cost of other prices yet. While the overall 3.1 inflation rate was high, core measures that strip out volatile items like oil were much lower and within the bank's target range."We haven't seen … a broader-based increase in prices, but I think that the bank has started to be concerned about what's coming down the road," Antunes told CBC News.And that concern is somewhat warranted, he said, especially after the bank didn't raise rates quickly in the face of high inflation post-COVID. The signal today is that the bank doesn't want a redo of that."I think the bank is concerned about this oil price shock playing a role here in the same way that it did in 2022. And you know, who can blame them? They're a little nervous about how that might play out."

Oil soars to US$103 per barrel, BoC sees no end in sight to war-linked inflationJeff LagerquistHere’s why you’re paying more for dieselCrude oil exports through the Strait of Hormuz are slowly recovering, so why is the price of diesel skyrocketing? The National's Eli Glasner breaks down what’s causing the increase, and why diesel prices likely won't drop anytime soon.Rising oil prices linked to war in the Middle East have been a persistent irritant for the Bank of Canada as it attempts to control inflation. That war could escalate in the coming weeks.U.S. officials have told several Gulf Arab countries to be prepared for a short, intense military campaign after the U.S. midterm elections on Nov. 3, the Wall Street Journal reported on Wednesday.The U.S. benchmark oil price soared nearly 3.5 per cent today, rising above $103 US per barrel. West Texas Intermediate crude is up nearly 70 per cent year-over-year. According to data from Kalibrate, Canadian pump prices for regular gasoline are up nearly 30 per cent on average versus this time last year. Diesel prices have soared over 70 per cent on an annualized basis.Here's what the Bank of Canada said about the situation earlier today:"The conflict in the Middle East is now in its eighth month, and there is no clear path to resolution. The combination of higher-for-longer energy prices, and increased pass-through, adds to the persistence of inflation in the projection."The prices of gasoline, diesel and heating oil are considerably higher than in July, and are expected to remain higher for longer. This is hitting consumers directly and raising business costs for production and transportation."

More hikes likely, but maybe not so soon: economistAbby HughesPeople pass the Bank of Montreal building in Toronto on Aug. 14, 2023. (Spencer Colby/The Canadian Press)Benjamin Reitzes, managing director at BMO Economics, says the central bank's messaging indicates further hikes will come — but maybe not soon.Despite the Bank of Canada warning that more rate hikes might be necessary, it also said it would proceed with caution. That "suggests a follow-up hike in December isn't a lock by any means," Reitzes said."There's likely more tightening to come, but the pace of further hikes is extremely uncertain and will be driven by the incoming data," he wrote in a note to investors.Reitzes says weak growth forecasted for the last few months of this year and continued trade uncertainty will be the things to watch — and that if momentum picks up there, that could trigger more increases.

Rate hike is bad news for businesses: CFIBAbby HughesSimon Gaudreault is the chief economist and vice-president of research at the Canadian Federation of Independent Business (CFIB). (Canadian Federation of Independent Business)Heading into today's decision, business owners across Canada were already in a tough spot. The trade war with the U.S. has been a significant weight and increased the cost of doing business, according to Simon Gaudreault, chief economist for the Canadian Federation of Independent Business (CFIB)."We're talking about entrepreneurs that have been entrepreneurs for 15, 20, 25 years or more, telling us that they've never seen such a challenging situation in terms of the operating costs," Gaudreault said.Today's rate hike could add to that pain for lots of businesses, he said. A rate hike would leave Canadian consumers with less cash in their pockets, which Gauldreaut says could hurt demand for business owners.Many business owners also have variable mortgages for business properties or hold other kinds of debt at floating rates, he said, meaning their costs will now be higher. It could also make it harder to take on new business investments, like upgrading equipment."The trade war hasn't brought that sort of certainty that you're looking for as an entrepreneur to invest. And so making the cost of capital even higher, even more expensive with the rate hike certainly won't help here."

Bank predict sluggish housing market, rate hike could dampen activityVerity StevensonBank of Canada's housing outlook 'pretty subdued' — but not just because of rates, official saysBank of Canada senior deputy governor Carolyn Rogers, speaking after the central bank hiked a key interest rate, said the organization's outlook for housing is 'pretty subdued' for a few reasons, including overall economic uncertainty.Deputy governor Carolyn Rogers acknowledged that the bank's interest rate hike will add to pressures on homebuyers."Certainly borrowing rates are currently weighing a bit on the housing market. An increase will add to that a bit on the margin," Rogers said.She said the bank expects Canada's housing market to remain sluggish over the next two years. Rogers said the bank's outlook for housing remains "pretty subdued," with growth forecast at about one per cent over the next two years."There's a number of things weighing on housing right now," Rogers said, pointing to broader uncertainty in the economy caused by inflation, energy costs and trade issues. "People don't tend to make big purchase decisions like housing in that kind of an environment."Rogers said the housing market is undergoing an adjustment, with particularly sharp slowdowns in British Columbia and Ontario, especially in Vancouver and Toronto.

Loonie wobbles post rate hike, expert sees 'weakness before the end of the year'Jeff LagerquistLoonies at the Royal Canadian Mint in Winnipeg on Nov. 14, 2023. (John Woods/The Canadian Press)The loonie is trading in a choppy fashion against U.S. dollar this morning, following the Bank of Canada's decision to hike its benchmark interest rate for the first time since July 2023.Canada's currency is currently worth $0.7124 US, according to Bloomberg data.Currency traders are struggling to reconcile the impact that higher borrowing costs could have on a still-weak Canadian economy, according to Karl Schamotta, chief market strategist at the payments company Corpay."Although we are bullish on the loonie over longer horizons, we remain convinced that markets are overpricing the Bank's tightening trajectory, and expect a bout of weakness before the end of the year as implied rate differentials widen against the currency again," he wrote in an online post on Wednesday.

Federal tax measures, major projects, higher oil exports expected to boost investmentVerity StevensonBank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem during today's news conference in Ottawa. (Adrian Wyld/The Canadian Press)Macklem was asked whether federal policies such as Carney's productivity mega deduction and the push to accelerate major projects improve the Canadian economic outlook. The governor said both those measures are predicted to help strengthen business investment in 2027, noting the economy is expected to grow by two per cent next year — a somewhat stronger outlook than the Bank of Canada had predicted in July. "There are some big projects through the Major Projects Office that will probably start to take shape next year. The mega deduction should support investment," Macklem said. The mega deduction, announced by Carney in September, allows companies to write off 100 per cent of the cost of eligible investments, such as machinery, from its taxable income in the year it becomes available for use, rather than deducting those costs gradually over several years. The bank predicts another factor will help the Canadian economy: Macklem said higher energy prices are also encouraging investment in Canada's oil and gas sector, with energy exports increasing.Still, Macklem cautioned that the bank has been relatively conservative in its assumptions about future investment."We've been disappointed in the past in investment in this country," he said. "We certainly think it'll be stronger. We'd like to be surprised it's even stronger than we've built in."

High oil costs out of Canada's control, so why hike?Abby HughesWhy now? Tiff Macklem asked what central bank aims to accomplish with rate hikeBank of Canada governor Tiff Macklem, when asked what the central bank was trying to accomplish with its first rate hike since 2023, acknowledged the complexity of the global economic situation, particularly around increased energy prices. But he said the policy rate — even with the increase — is 'low enough that it's not restraining growth' but will help get inflation back to target 'more quickly.'Because inflation is being driven by high oil prices — which are out of Canada's control — a reporter asked Macklem what he hoped to achieve by raising interest rates.Macklem said the goal with the rate hike is to contain inflation and prevent high energy costs from upping the cost of other products Canadians would buy at stores.As oil prices have been elevated for months on end with no end in sight, Macklem said businesses have indicated in the bank's surveys that they intend to pass on some of those energy costs to consumers. "Canadians are already paying for more at the pump. And we can't … change that," Macklem said. But what would be worse is if Canadians had to "pay for it twice" because of that passthrough.He says the hike is low enough that it shouldn't hamper growth too much but should also help get inflation back to its target range more quickly.

articles.title: What we know so far about deadly Spain train crash
articles.summary: More than 500 passengers were on board the trains when the incident occurred in the province of Toledo, south of Madrid.

blocks.text: Spanish Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez said he was "shocked by the serious train accident in Toledo".

"I remain in constant contact with the Minister of Transport, and with the president of Castilla-La Mancha," Sánchez said on X, adding that emergency services were working on the ground "to assist those affected and ensure their safety, in coordination with all the involved administrations".
"My affection, solidarity, and support to all the victims and their families."
Sánchez and other Spanish politicians have cancelled all public engagements on Wednesday, including campaigning for next month's parliamentary elections.
Spain's royal family posted on X that it was "shocked and concerned" by the accident and expressed condolences for the relatives of the deceased and those affected by the crash.
A huge emergency response is under way with fire crews and helicopters at the scene.
Spanish news agency have reported that hospitals in the area have suspended planned surgeries as they deal with an influx of patients from the crash.

A blood transfusion centre in Madrid has also appealed for "urgent" donations. In a post on X, Centro de Transfusión said it made the request "in the face of a possible sudden increase in care needs".
It reported that facilities in Toledo, Ciudad Real and Alcázar de San Juan have cancelled procedures as casualties from the crash begin to arrive.
This is the second high-speed rail tragedy in Spain this year.
In January a high-speed train derailed in southern Spain, its rear carriages going into the path of a state-run Renfe train, claiming the lives of 46 people.

articles.title: Judge rules Trump-appointed US prosecutor in Los Angeles is not serving legally – US politics live
articles.summary: Department of Justice says it intends to appeal as administration tries to keep president’s ally Bill Essayli in office

blocks.text: Federal judge rules Trump-appointed US prosecutor in Los Angeles isn't legally serving
Hello and welcome to the US politics live blog.
A federal judge has ruled that Republican Bill Essayli is not legally serving as the top US prosecutor in Los Angeles.
Essayli was disqualified from overseeing two criminal prosecutions. The order, however, will not immediately go into effect, and the Department of Justice (DoJ) has said it intends to appeal.
The ruling was part of a long-running legal battle challenging the Trump administration’s maneuvers to keep Essayli in office despite not being confirmed by the US Senate.

Essayli, a former Republican state lawmaker and ally of Donald Trump, became an interim US attorney in April 2025, but he was not formally nominated by the president, which allowed him to lead the office without going through the standard confirmation process.

After Essayli’s “interim” appointment ended last July, the Trump administration gave him an “acting” title, then kept him on as a “first assistant” after a judge ruled he was unlawfully serving as US attorney.

But in August, a federal appellate court ruled against a Nevada justice department leader in a similar case, and the judge overseeing Essayli’s case cited that higher court’s ruling on Tuesday, issuing another order saying he was still acting unlawfully.

Michael Seabright, the federal judge, said Essayli was illegally serving, even with a “special attorney” and “first assistant” designation by the Trump administration, and the judge said he could no longer participate in or supervise two ongoing prosecutions where the attorneys had challenged his position.

“We respectfully disagree with the court’s order,” Essayli said in a statement on Tuesday. “The President and the Attorney General have every right to select supervisors within the Justice Department.”

In other developments:

items: Faced with widespread voter discontent over the spike in oil prices since he attacked Iran, Donald Trump staged his rally in Corpus Christi, Texas on Tuesday alongside a vast oil tanker, the Angerona, which, the president said, had just arrived from Venezuela bearing a personal gift for him: a million barrels of oil.

blocks.text: Key events

items: 30m agoFederal judge rules Trump-appointed US prosecutor in Los Angeles isn't legally serving

blocks.text: Gaya Gupta

The US Federal Reserve is expected to leave interest rates unchanged on Wednesday during its last rate-setting meeting before the midterm elections, keeping rates at one of the highest pre-election levels seen in over 20 years.

Last month, Fed officials raised rates for the first time since 2023, citing rising inflation. Inflation has hovered for years above the Fed’s target rate of 2%, and for most of this year, the annualized inflation rate has remained above 3%.
The move infuriated Donald Trump, who said that “interest rates in the United States should be 1% or less”.
Though inflation rose higher in September, going from 3.4% in August to 3.7%, a pause would signal the central bank is taking a wait-and-see approach ahead of the midterms next week.
Interest rates determine the cost of interest for loans, including for credit cards, mortgage and some savings accounts. During times of high inflation, raising rates can slow price increases.
Multiple Fed leaders have suggested in recent weeks that the central bank has room for a pause, even if most Fed economists are predicting one more rate hike before the end of the year.
“The hikes do not need to come at consecutive meetings, but they should be in place in an acceptable period of time,” Fed governor Christopher Waller said earlier this month.

items: Faced with widespread voter discontent over the spike in oil prices since he attacked Iran, Donald Trump staged his rally in Corpus Christi, Texas on Tuesday alongside a vast oil tanker, the Angerona, which, the president said, had just arrived from Venezuela bearing a personal gift for him: a million barrels of oil.
A senior State Department official told the Associated Press that the US will “will issue visas to Flávio Bolsonaro and his family and allow them entry into the United States”.

In his remarks to supporters in Lubbock, Texas, Trump attacked James Talarico, the Democratic nominee for Senate, for having shown compassion for transgender children who demonstrated for their rights at the Texas state capitol in 2023.

articles.title: Flávio Bolsonaro on flight to Miami after fleeing Brazil following election defeat
articles.summary:
Far-right senator and family expected to land in US after crossing into Argentina and then flying out of Ecuador

A jet carrying the far-right Brazilian senator Flávio Bolsonaro has left…

blocks.text: A jet carrying the far-right Brazilian senator Flávio Bolsonaro has left Guayaquil in Ecuador and is on its way to Miami, Florida, where it is expected to arrive mid-morning on Wednesday.

After losing Sunday night’s election to the incumbent president, Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva, Bolsonaro disappeared for more than 24 hours, until Argentina’s migration authorities said he had entered the country by land on Tuesday night.

There, he boarded a Gulfstream IV registered as LV-JQW. The aircraft had been parked at Puerto Iguazú airport since the early hours of the previous morning, when the first reports emerged in Argentinian media that he intended to flee on it.

Bolsonaro, the son of the jailed former Brazilian president Jair Bolsonaro, boarded the jet with his wife and two daughters at about 11.30pm, bound for Guayaquil, reportedly to avoid Brazilian airspace. They made a brief stop in Ecuador, and have continued to the Miami-Opa Locka executive airport. The senator is expected to hold a press conference in the US at some point on Wednesday.

A senior US state department official told media outlets that visas would be granted to Bolsonaro and his family, and on Tuesday night the US president said he would approve their move to the country.

blocks.caption: Brazil’s president, Luiz Inacio Lula da Silva, greets supporters while celebrating his birthday and re-election. Photograph: Pablo Porciúncula/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: “They’re fine people. The election was very strange, and I thought it was terrible,” Donald Trump said, as he returned from a campaign event in Texas. “I didn’t take sides, you know. I know them both. I know Lula. I know Flavio a little bit. I know the father very well.”

Lula called Bolsonaro’s flight “shameful”. “This is what the Bolsonaro family are like. Brazil is their second homeland. Their first homeland is licking the boots of the US, as they’ve become accustomed to doing,” he said at an event celebrating his 81st birthday in Brasília.

Some in the Brazilian government suspected Bolsonaro allies had spent Tuesday privately telling the press he was already on his way to the US to distract from his real plan through Argentina. The federal police are facing criticism for failing to prevent him leaving the country.

There is a gap between the last time he was seen by allies at about 6pm on Monday and the moment he entered Argentina late on Tuesday. It remains unclear how or when he travelled to the border, or where he was during that time.
Footage from a television channel there shows two vans crossing the border checkpoint and then being escorted by airport security officers to the airport.

Shortly after the election result, police asked the supreme court to order Bolsonaro’s passport to be retained over concerns he could flee, citing an interview given last Friday by his brother, the former congressman Eduardo Bolsonaro.

Speaking on a podcast in the US, where he is in self-imposed exile and lobbying the Trump administration against Lula, Eduardo said if his brother were to lose the election, he should not concede and should go to the US.

O Globo newspaper reported that the escape had been planned for weeks as a contingency in case he lost, and that Eduardo had been its main organiser, holding talks with US officials about receiving the senator.

articles.title: Coalition talks loom in Israel as Netanyahu and Eisenkot blocs set to fall short of majority
articles.summary: Projections show votes for Palestinian parties surged in a tight contest that saw the highest turnout in decades

blocks.text: Israel’s future hung in the balance on Wednesday morning as it became clear that Benjamin Netanyahu had lost his governing majority, and his political fate now depends on whether opposition Jewish parties are prepared to forge a common front with Palestinian parties, whose support surged in Tuesday’s elections.

The leader of the Jewish opposition bloc, the retired general Gadi Eisenkot, appeared to rule out such a broad coalition in a premature declaration of victory overnight for what he called a “Zionist majority”.

As the vote count proceeded on Wednesday, initial exit poll projections that Eisenkot’s bloc would have a narrow lead over Netanyahu’s coalition looked increasingly in doubt as the prime minister’s bloc edged ahead, with the votes of deployed soldiers and other absentee ballots yet to be counted.

With 70% of votes counted, both Jewish blocs looked certain to fall short of the 61 Knesset seats needed for a majority government, leaving Eisenkot and his allies facing a clear choice: either make a pact with Arab Israeli parties heading for a record result of 16-19 seats, or hand Netanyahu a political lifeline in the form of new elections or a unity government.

Donald Trump took credit for Netanyahu’s better than expected performance so far, claiming his overt backing in the run-up to the vote had made the difference. “When the endorsement went out, it helped him a lot,” Trump said, adding that the result appeared to be heading for a stalemate or a Netanyahu win.

blocks.caption: Benjamin Netanyahu at the Likud party election night event in Jerusalem. Photograph: Alexi J Rosenfeld/Getty Images

blocks.text: Yair Golan, the leader of the centre-left Democrats, a junior partner in Eisenkot’s Change bloc, urged Eisenkot to negotiate with the two Palestinian parties, the Joint List and Ra’am (the United Arab List).

“We have no future here if we don’t stop being afraid. And if we don’t put an end to racism. We can no longer accept Netanyahu’s racist distinction between Jewish and Arab votes,” Golan said in a post on X.

“Anyone who tries to erase the votes of Arab citizens is surrendering to Netanyahu and giving up on Israel,” he added, pointing out that Netanyahu relied on ultra-Orthodox Jewish parties that were non-Zionist and opposed conscription for their constituents.

Noa Landau, a commenter writing in Haaretz, argued that by making Zionism the test for forming a coalition, excluding potential partners, while the prime minister had not, Eisenkot had fallen “into the trap Netanyahu laid for him over the course of the election campaign”.

The Joint List leader, Yousef Jabareen, said its strong performance meant it “can’t be ignored under any political scenario”. He said Netanyahu’s government, especially its extremist national security minister, Itamar Ben-Gvir, “has made life bitter for every Arab citizen”.

“We will be ready to pave the way to oust the government of Netanyahu, Ben-Gvir and Smotrich – and send them home,” Jabareen said. Another Joint List official described the choice facing the Jewish opposition as “supremacy or building democracy”.

blocks.caption: Gadi Eisenkot at an election night rally in Tel Aviv. Photograph: Jack Guez/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Counting all the votes could take another few days, with absentee ballots the last to be tallied. Most of those are from deployed soldiers. The army vote usually swings right, but that broad picture may be complicated by the fact that a lot of older, more moderate reservists are now on active duty.

Once all the votes are accounted for, it will be up to Israel’s president, Isaac Herzog, to give one of the party leaders six weeks to form a government. If the first choice fails, the opportunity passes to his rival. In the weeks of political wrangling likely to ensue, both Netanyahu and Eisenkot are expected to lure defectors from each other’s camps.

Netanyahu would remain in office in a caretaker capacity until a new majority is formed. He might expect to benefit if the deadlock leads to another round of elections. Tens of thousands of diaspora Israelis who returned to vote on Tuesday, and were mostly opposed to the governing coalition, might not return for another vote, for example.

Tuesday’s election came as Israel is fighting accusations of genocide in Gaza and ethnic cleansing of Palestinians in the West Bank. Netanyahu is separately wanted by the international criminal court for alleged war crimes.

The election was widely seen as a referendum on the 77-year-old leader, and the vote drew 77.7% turnout, the highest since 1999, with marked increases in the number of serving military members voting.

blocks.caption: Netanyahu supporters celebrate in the early hours of Wednesday.  Photograph: John Wessels/AFP/Getty Images

blocks.text: Political deadlock has led to repeated votes in the past. Between 2019 and 2022, Israel held five elections.

Netanyahu is Israel’s longest-serving prime minister, governing for 19 of the past 30 years, and its most tenacious political survivor. Entangled in a long-running corruption trial, Netanyahu and his far-right coalition had stoked xenophobic fears and suggested Israel would be vulnerable to a nuclear attack without him.
The campaign, febrile even by Israeli standards, included Netanyahu posting a picture of a nuclear explosion devastating Tel Aviv on the eve of the polls opening.

Since the deadly attack launched by Hamas on Israel’s southern communities on 7 October 2023, Israel has devastated Gaza and killed more than 74,000 Palestinians, fought Hezbollah in Lebanon, occupied new territory in Syria and launched a war with the US against Iran.

articles.title: [Mind the Gap] In chaotic US midterm polls, Filams are running
articles.summary: Filipinos running across statewide and local races find themselves navigating an American political system increasingly resembling tactics they thought they had left behind

blocks.text: It’s hard not to feel that this November 2026 US midterm elections is a déjà vu of cheating in Philippine elections.

“Dinaya!” is usually the first word a losing candidate shouts in the Philippines: “I got cheated!” President Donald Trump seems to have taken this script to heart, casting a shadow over the forecasted “Blue Wave” that could flip Congress to Democratic control even before the first ballot is counted.

Even if Trump’s unfounded claims of voter fraud are overwhelmed by a huge Democratic turnout, many fear that Republicans in Congress, out of loyalty to Trump, may try to block Democrats from assuming the majority.

Echoing the “doomsday scenario” espoused by US Attorney General Todd Blanche — delaying the count or refusing to certify results if they favor Democrats — Trump has directed the Justice Department to block certification of the coming Senate election in Alaska if Republican incumbent Dan S. Sullivan loses by a narrow margin. The New York Times reported that the justice department cited flimsy concerns about confusion with another candidate whose name is similar to Sullivan’s.

Their efforts to project a narrative of widespread noncitizen voting is also relentless, even using as bogeymen the 11 individuals the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) who were arrested in California on October 16 for allegedly illegally registering to vote. Election experts have raised questions as to whether the charges could be trusted to be accurate, citing similar accusations being disproved elsewhere in the country.

Remember when Gloria Macapagal-Arroyo called “Hello, Garci!” to pad her votes during the 2004 presidential election against the late Fernando Poe Jr.? Trump seems to have taken a page from that “Dagdag-Bawas” playbook by questioning voter registrations, challenging mail-in ballots and raising the possibility of hacking voting machines.

“My thought was they could keep it in their back pocket to invalidate any election results they don’t like,” a former Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) official told ProPublica, which reported that DHS has asked CISA to “secretly acquire a voting machine and hack it.”

With early voting underway, shaving off Democrat votes is in play, with software glitches delaying nearly 600,000 voter registrations in Texas. In Nashville, Tennessee, Dolly Parton’s sister, singer Stella Parton, claimed she had to correct her ballot multiple times, saying a voting machine repeatedly selected Republican gubernatorial candidate Marsha Blackburn when she tried to vote for Democrat Jerri Green.

While a seasoned “trapo” in the Philippines rolls a ₱1,000 note in a folded T-shirt to buy votes, Trump is dangling $5,000 to voters and billions in federal aid to farmers affected by tariffs if Republicans keep control of Congress.

While hired armed goons in the Philippines steal ballot boxes, Trump has threatened to send heavily-armed ICE agents and National Guard troops to polling places, raising fears of intimidation among immigrant and minority voters. Though we are hopefully far from the impunity of an “Ampatuan massacre,” the shocking, pre-dawn DHS raid on Representative Ilhan Omar’s home three weeks before election day smacks of the same tactic in eliminating his political enemies.

Amid this chaos, Filipino candidates running across statewide and local races find themselves navigating an American political system increasingly resembling tactics they thought they had left behind.

This year’s crop includes California Attorney General Rob Bonta, seeking reelection; Assemblymember Jessica Caloza, fighting to retain her 52nd District seat; and Cerritos City Councilmember Mark Pulido, campaigning for the 67th Assembly District in the California state legislature.

In Daly City, Councilmember Rod Daus-Magbual is running for reelection, joined by Tony Bayudan in what is often celebrated as the “Pinoy Capital” of the United States, where Filipinos make up a full third of the population. In Southern California, Artesia Councilmember Melissa Ramoso is defending her seat while Los Angeles City Controller Kenneth Mejia seeks a second term.
The Filipino political footprint extends beyond California.

In Nevada, Assemblymember Erica Mosca is seeking reelection. In New York, Assemblymember Steven Raga is running for State Senate in Queens, while Georgia State Representative Marvin Lim is running unopposed.

Across the Pacific, Hawaii — the first state to elect a Filipino governor in US history with the landmark 1994 election of Benjamin Cayetano — has its own growing crop of FilAm candidates. State Senator Joy A. San Buenaventura is seeking reelection in Puna, joined by State House candidates including Tess Abalos, Travis Bumanglag, Danny Degracia, Diamond Garcia, Greggor Ilagan, Darius K. Kila, Rose Martinez and Julie Reyes Oda.

blocks.caption: 4 ways US foreign policy could change if Democrats win in November

blocks.text: At the county level, Tyler Dos Santos-Tam is seeking another term on the Honolulu City Council, while Kauanoe Batangan and Addison Bulosan are running for county council seats on Maui and Kauai.
It’s time for us to walk precincts, man phone banks and donate to our kababayan running for office.

We immigrated to the United States to escape the feudal dynasties, vote-buying and the “Guns, Goons and Gold” of traditional Philippine politics. Now it’s time to push back and make sure those tactics don’t follow us here.
So, don’t forget to vote. If voting in person, carefully review your selections before submitting your ballot to make sure the machine properly records your choice.
If voting by mail, don’t wait until November 3 to mail your ballots to prevent the understaffed US Postal Service from throwing them away if they don’t get picked up on Election Day.

In one of the most consequential elections in modern history, our mission this November is not only in supporting our kababayan to win — it is a front-line battle to make sure our votes are counted, and defend them if need be. – Rappler.com
Oscar Quiambao is a former reporter for The Philippine Daily Inquirer who now lives in San Francisco.

articles.title: Can we regrow damaged seagrass meadows?
articles.summary: Seagrass protects coasts, shelters thousands of species and stores CO2. But some 30% of this valuable ecosystem has disappeared since the late 19th century. Can we bring it back?

image.caption: Regrowing underwater seagrass meadows takes time and patienceImage: Geomar

blocks.text: Half a dozen divers are navigating the cold waters of the Baltic Sea off the coast of Dahme, a small beach town in northern Germany. Keeping the roots intact, conservationists carefully lift shoots from a donor meadow of seagrass and place them in a bag.

They only take a few shoots from each spot, which will be planted where the conservationists hope to regrow another meadow. They've already picked out a prime area for the young plants, which need sandy sediment, shelter from waves and currents and sufficient light and oxygen to thrive.

The scientists see the work as critical. Myriam Spicka, who heads the NGO Seagrass Conservation, says she has "seen the changes" in the more than 30 years she's been diving. And she is not the only one who has witnessed the destruction.
How seagrass is becoming a green building material
Scientists estimate that around 60% of the Baltic coast's seagrass meadows have disappeared.
"That's the bad news," said marine ecologist Thorsten Reusch from the GEOMAR Helmholtz Center for Ocean Research Kiel . "The good news is that the decline has stopped."
Why should we care about seagrass?

Underwater seagrass meadows feed and shelter fish, crabs, shellfish and many other species. They improve water quality and slow waves, helping protect shores from erosion. And they store carbon in the seabed about 30 to 50 times faster than forests.
Around 70 species of seagrass can be found along the coasts of more than 150 countries. Some grow just below the surface, others at depths of 60 meters or almost 200 feet.
On patrol with Mallorca's 'seagrass police'
"Some countries have far more seagrass, particularly in the Indo-Pacific," said Reusch. "There, it can play a major role in their carbon balance."

But the value of seagrass goes beyond carbon storage. Its meadows in the Baltic are among the sea's most valuable habitats. They shelter wildlife, stabilize the seabed and act as natural filters by trapping particles and nutrients.
How can seagrass be replanted on a larger scale?
Planting individual seagrass shoots is painstaking work so people like Reinhard Helbig are trying to make it easier.

Through ZosteraTec, the start-up he co-founded, he helps restore marine habitats, including seagrass meadows damaged by offshore activity, such as wind farm construction. His work begins on the beach.
"Stormy weather helps us. Waves and currents wash seagrass out of the seabed. A day or two later, it washes up here, still fresh," he said.

blocks.caption: The pressed strand of seagrass with biodegradable thread makes it easier to plant on longer stretches along the ocean floorImage: DW

blocks.text: The collected shoots are grown and multiplied in ZosteraTec's aquaculture. Several months later, the marine saplings are laid on a plant support. A specially developed machine binds the planted strands with biodegradable thread. The resulting lengths can be laid on the seabed with less diving work.
"We plant here on land to cut down on underwater work. That means fewer dives, and we can do the painstaking work on shore," Helbig said.
Could planting seeds be a solution?
Researchers at the Geomar Helmholtz Center in Kiel are also testing new ways to restore seagrass across larger areas, including using seeds.
Marine ecologist Esther Thomsen reaches into an aquarium tank and pulls out a flowerpot containing seagrass.
"Ten percent of the plants in our meadows produce seeds. You can clearly see the seeds sitting inside the seed pod," she said.
"The big advantage of restoring meadows from seed is greater genetic diversity. And in the future, we should be able to sow seeds over much larger areas," explained Thomsen.

blocks.caption: Together with replanted shoots, seeds can help regrow underwater meadowsImage: DW

blocks.text: Reusch from Geomar said they currently "think the most promising way to grow meadows that can withstand climate change is to plant individual shoots as a foundation, then sow seeds between them to increase genetic diversity."
It takes time to see results
Whether a planting mission is successful is revealed months or even years later.

Thomsen and her colleagues are visiting the first seagrass meadow planted in Germany's Baltic waters in 2021. The divers count shoots, check how densely they grow and record how the meadow has developed.
They then compare it with the donor meadow that supplied the plants. Only that comparison reveals whether the new crop has merely survived or is beginning to function more like a natural one.
"We've just checked the seagrass meadow, and it's really dense. We counted lots of shoots per square," Thomsen said. "It's looking really good."
This article is based on a Global Us video report.

articles.title: DepEd welcomes parents helping secure schools
articles.summary: The Department of Education (DepEd) on Wednesday welcomed proposals for parents to help patrol schools as authorities step up security measures following a series of school shootings in recent months.

blocks.text: Published October 28, 2026 6:39pm

The Department of Education (DepEd) on Wednesday welcomed proposals for parents to help patrol schools as authorities step up security measures following a series of school shootings in recent months.

In a media interview, Education Secretary Sonny Angara said parental involvement in school security could also help address other concerns affecting students, including mental health and social media use.

“Welcome po sa amin yun. Dahil pinapakita yun na involved sila dito sa paaralan at pagka-nandito sila as security, magiging concerned din sila sa ibang bagay, yung mental health, yung paggamit ng social media, so wine-welcome natin yung tulong ng ating mga parents at yan talaga ang pakay ng Kaagapay program po natin,” he said.

(We welcome that because it shows that parents are involved in the school. When they participate in security efforts, they also become concerned about other matters, such as mental health and social media use. We welcome their help, as that is the purpose of our Kaagapay program.)
The Kaagapay program is a DepEd initiative aimed at encouraging greater parental involvement in their children's learning and development.

Angara made the statement after inspecting Lakan Dula High School in Tondo, Manila, as part of a school safety audit. He described the school as a model for safety, citing its security cameras, metal detectors and medical equipment.
The school also has a community drop box and a QR (quick response) code through which students and teachers can anonymously report their concerns.
The agency has since strengthened school safety and security protocols in response to the incidents of school-related violence.

In June, two students reportedly opened fire on their classmates at a high school in Tacloban, killing three people. Less than two months later, another school shooting in Zamboanga City left two students dead.
In September, a student shot two schoolmates before turning the gun on himself in South Cotabato.
The incidents shocked a country where school shootings have been extremely rare. The government has cited online groomers and nihilistic violent extremism as possible factors behind the attacks.
According to Angara, coordination with social media platform Meta was still ongoing following the incidents.
He also urged parents to take an active role in their children's lives at home.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: EU's 'Made in Europe' push unnerves global auto suppliers
articles.summary: In shielding Europe's carmakers from Chinese rivals, the EU risks hurting close partners from Turkey and Morocco to Japan and South Korea. Billions in trade and hundreds of thousands of European jobs…

image.caption: As well as supplying vehicles and parts to the EU, Turkey is making its own electric carsImage: Murat Cetinmuhurdar/Turkish Presidency/HandoutAA/picture alliance

blocks.text: It is meant to save Europe's auto industry from China's unfair trade practices. The European Union's Industrial Accelerator Act (IAA), proposed in March, seeks to upgrade European car factories and only subsidize vehicles produced in Europe.

Yet, the EU's "Made in Europe" plan is causing deep concern among other allied carmaking nations — such as Turkey, Morocco, Japan and South Korea — all of them deeply embedded in European supply chains.

After months of deadlock over the IAA's potential impact on their own vehicle production, Germany and France earlier this month reached a key compromise that would allow suppliers from non-EU members like the United Kingdom and Norway to qualify for "European origin" status.
The legacy car industry is in crisis. How can it move on?
Close to Europe, but not close enough
Other key players in the automotive sector, however, will be excluded — including Turkey, which has enjoyed seamless access to the EU market since the mid-1990s.

While the proposals still face major legislative hurdles in Brussels before becoming law, Ayhan Zeytinoglu, chairman of the Economic Development Foundation (IKV), thinks the Franco-German framework could be devastating for Turkey's auto sector.

"73% of Turkey’s total automotive exports go to the EU," Zeytinoglu told DW. "If we encounter a 'Made in Europe' barrier in the EU market, this will cause great damage to our trade with the EU and to our exports."
Excluding Turkey would also harm European automaking rather than strengthen competitiveness against China, he added.
Turkey's auto exporters association OIB calculated that the country's automotive exports to the EU totaled $30.1 billion (€26.8 billion) last year.
Protecting auto parts made in Europe
The IAA requires that 70% of the total value of a vehicle's components — excluding the battery — should be made in Europe.
However, the initial proposal only applies to battery-electric vehicles (EVs), plug-in hybrids and fuel-cell models, which last year made up just 27% of all new EU car registrations.

Tommaso Pardi, director of the international automotive research network GERPISA and a senior researcher at the French National Center for Scientific Research (CNRS), notes that the 70% target is remarkably generous.
"If you take an average European-made electric car and take away the battery, you would find that around 83% [of parts] come from Europe," Pardi told DW.
Under the revised German-French plan, some self-charging hybrids and petrol and diesel vehicles could still be sold after 2035 and would also be affected by the "Made in Europe" rules.
These cars contain a much lower proportion of European parts. Most of Turkey's nearly 800,000 vehicle exports to the EU last year would fall under this much larger umbrella.
Europe's EV battery problem: Can it catch up with China?
China seeks a side entrance
Another key reason for excluding Turkey is that Chinese automakers are expanding their presence there, hoping to gain back-door access to the EU market, but face major roadblocks.
They include SWM Motors, whose factory in the northwestern city of Eskisehir closed within a year because the cars produced didn't meet EU safety standards.
BYD's plans to open a $1 billion plant in Manisa — a large industrial hub near the Aegean coast — have been put on hold.

Morocco, meanwhile, has received Chinese investments worth more than €10 billion ($11 billion) since the COVID-19 pandemic, according to consultancy AlixPartners, much of it in batteries and auto parts.

For France, the North African nation plays a similar role to China for Germany's auto sector — a low-cost production hub that helps French carmakers stay competitive. Budget-friendly French models would likely become more expensive if Morocco were excluded.

Japanese carmakers, which build several of their models in European factories, could also lose out. Cars imported from Japan would not qualify for EU subsidies, while models built in France, Portugal and Eastern Europe would benefit only if enough of their parts come from Europe.

South Korean automakers, meanwhile, could also be hurt. Hyundai and Kia build cars in the Czech Republic and Slovakia, but also ship models from Asia, which would not qualify. Korean battery plants in Poland and Hungary, however, would count as European.

blocks.caption: Morocco's auto plants are helping keep the costs of French car brands downImage: Renault/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Carmakers fight to keep cheap imports
Pardi notes how European car giants are actively lobbying to water down the IAA to protect their high profit margins.
"They want to limit the IAA to retain the biggest scope to still source from abroad, particularly from China," he said.
EU-based automakers warn that higher parts costs would put them at an even bigger disadvantage against Chinese rivals, while European battery supply is unlikely to meet demand anytime soon.
Ankara is also lobbying Brussels to be included in the "Made in Europe" scheme, while automakers are seeking a compromise that would allow Turkey to join at a later stage.
Pardi said this would be "only for European companies that are based there [Turkey and Morocco] ... while excluding all recent investments involving Chinese capital [in those countries]."
EU to weaken combustion engine ban amid industry pressure
'Stop the bleeding' say auto parts suppliers

European auto-parts suppliers are, however, on the opposite side of the argument, calling for further strengthening of IAA. They warn that up to 650,000 auto jobs in the region could be lost by 2035 without better protection for their members.

"A lost industrial job is very hard to win back, and the damage reaches well beyond large suppliers," Benjamin Krieger, Secretary General of the European Association of Automotive Suppliers (CLEPA), told DW.
Krieger thinks the IAA helps European industry to level the playing field against unfair competition from China, adding: "We must stop the bleeding."

With broad public support for measures that ensure that EU public funding "benefits value creation in Europe," CLEPA's Krieger thinks allies like Turkey, Morocco, South Korea and Japan may not lose out if they meet the EU's criteria.

"The EU should offer access to the IAA through an opt-in mechanism with objective criteria: regulatory alignment, social and environmental standards, no market distortion, respect for the rule of law and reciprocity, backed by anti-circumvention measures. Partners that meet them are welcome," he said.
Additional reporting by Aram Ekin Duran.

blocks.text: Geman Chancellor Friedrich Merz said Germany and Japan would explore jointly developing a fighter jet as they seek closer industrial ties.

articles.title: Tanzania celebrates first natural gas discovery in more than 10 years
articles.summary: The energy minister described it as a "major milestone" for the East African nation.

blocks.text: "The discovery is important in ensuring the country has reliable, clean and safe energy at affordable costs, particularly at a time when demand is increasing due to industrial growth and other economic activities," Homera said.
Natural gas accounted for nearly 80% of Tanzania's sources of electricity generation, according to government statistics for 2024.
In recent years, the country has also encouraged the use of compressed natural gas to power vehicles, with natural gas plants and filling stations set up mostly in the largest city, Dar es Salaam.
Some Tanzanians have been converting their vehicles to a dual-fuel system - with the locally available natural gas allowing for cheaper prices than petrol.
Tanzania made its first natural gas discovery in 1974 on the Songo Songo Island in the south-east Lindi region, followed by a second discovery at Mnazi Bay in neighbouring region of Mtwara in 1982.

The commercialisation of these discoveries began in 2004. This propelled further gas exploration both onshore and offshore, with the largest single discovery of 2.7 trillion cubic feet of natural gas in 2016.

articles.title: Serbian shot dead after attacking officer outside Israeli embassy, minister says
articles.summary: Authorities say the attacker in Belgrade was an underage male who was being monitored by security services.

blocks.text: Serbian police shot dead a young man outside the Israeli embassy in Belgrade in the early hours of Wednesday after what authorities called a "terrorist attack".

The country's interior minister, Ivica Dacic, said the attacker had rushed at a police officer with two knives while shouting the phrase "Allahu Akbar". The officer sustained a minor knife wound to the face and shot the attacker.
Dacic said the suspect has not been identified, but he was a minor and Serbian citizen who was being monitored by security services as he was "known to be a supporter of the Islamic State".
Speaking to reporters outside the embassy, Dacic said an investigation is ongoing, but security services said the suspect had posted a picture of the Islamic State flag on his Instagram.

Dacic raised the country's terrorism threat level to "red alert" - the highest threat level – meaning stricter security checks and increased police presence at places like infrastructure facilities and areas where large crowds gather.
The interior minister said he had visited the injured police officer, who was reportedly doing well and did not need hospital care for his wounds.
Armed security personnel were seen standing guard outside the Israeli embassy on Wednesday morning.
Israel's foreign ministry confirmed in a social media post that no embassy personnel were injured and the mission was closed at the time of the incident.
This is the second such attack on Belgrade's Israeli embassy in less than three years; in June 2024, a man shot a police officer in the neck with a crossbow.
The officer who was shot survived the attack and shot dead the assailant, identified as a Serbian man who had converted to Islam.
Wednesday's attack comes just one day after elections in Israel.

articles.title: At least 10 dead in crash between 2 trains in central Spain, authorities say
articles.summary: A high-speed train slammed into the rear of another train that had stopped, derailing two cars and killing at least 10 people on Wednesday in central Spain, authorities said.

image.caption: The scene of a collision between two trains in Urda, Spain, on Wednesday. Local authorities say at least 10 people have died, but the figure is expected to rise. (Juanma Jimenez/Europa Press/The Associated Press)

blocks.text: World·Breaking
A high-speed train slammed into the rear of another train that had stopped, derailing two cars and killing at least 10 people on Wednesday in central Spain, authorities said.
Rail service was suspended between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia
Esther Padilla, spokesperson for the Castilla La Mancha region, said authorities can confirm 10 deaths, but that "that number will surely rise."
Spain's rail system operator ADIF said the crash occurred Wednesday morning in the province of Toledo. Rail service was suspended between Madrid, Ciudad Real and Andalusia.

Padilla told state broadcaster TVE that the accident was between two high-speed trains heading in the same direction from Madrid to Seville and that one ran into the tail of the other while it was stopped, knocking two of its cars off the track. She said the cause of the crash was not known.
The accident involved a train from Spain's state-owned RENFE company and the private rail company IRYO. Trains from those two companies were also involved in a deadly crash in January.
Padilla said that 397 passengers were in the RENFE train and 147 passengers in the IRYO train.

items: Death toll climbs to 39 in high-speed train collision in Spain

blocks.text: The mayor of the nearby town of Urda, Manuel Galán, told Spanish state broadcaster TVE that passengers had been injured and that civil protection authorities had asked his town hall to prepare a sports pavilion to attend to passengers.
The regional president of Castilla La Mancha, Emiliano García-Page, wrote on X that he is on his way to the crash site.

In January, 45 people died in southern Spain when a train jumped the track and hit an oncoming train. The crash was the deadliest in Spain since a 2013 crash that killed 80 people. The January incident shook the confidence the European country has in its extensive high-speed rail network.

articles.title: Vapes and cigarettes? Cop denies knowledge of Laos drug shipment try
articles.summary: The policewoman who was reportedly linked with the attempted smuggling of P3.5 billion worth of shabu from Laos to the Philippines said she had no knowledge that the shipment contained illegal drugs.

blocks.text: Published October 28, 2026 6:11pm
The policewoman who was reportedly linked with the attempted smuggling of P3.5 billion worth of shabu from Laos to the Philippines said she had no knowledge that the shipment contained illegal drugs.

During the Senate committee on public services, Police Master Sergeant Aileen Jane Mendoza admitted that she looked for an aircraft that could be rented to transport the cargo, but she believed it only contained vapes and cigarettes.
Senator Raffy Tulfo, chairperson of the committee, asked the police officer if she knew that such shipment was illegal.
"Ang alam ko po, Mr. Chair, may kaukulang requirements po na magbabayad po kung sino ang consignee dito sa atin sa Pilipinas," said Mendoza, who attended the hearing online.
(What I know, Mr. Chair, is that there were corresponding requirements that must be paid by the consignee here in the Philippines.)

"Wala naman pong facilitation na nangyari sa ginawa ko. Ang ginawa ko po kasi, naghanap po ako ng aircraft na mare-rentahan. Regarding sa facilitation, hindi na po kasi ako ang taong in charge du'n after ko maghanap ng aircraft," she added.
(There was no facilitation in what I did. What I did was look for an aircraft to rent. After that, my job was done and I was no longer in charge of the facilitation.)
Mendoza also said she did not inform her supervisor, Police Colonel Joanna Zarcilla, regarding the chartered flight that was supposed to arrive in Manila from Laos.
Tulfo said Zarcilla should be investigated as well, while recommending her suspension pending the result of the probe.
The senator expressed belief that there may be a conspiracy among those involved in the processing of chartered flights.

"Ang pinag-uusapan natin dito ay bilyon—P3.54 billion. Hindi ako maniniwala na walang sabwatan dito hanggang sa kataas-taasan diyan kung saan mang ahensyang involved sa pag-process nitong chartered flights," Tulfo said.
(We are talking about billions here—P3.54 billion. I won't believe that there is no collusion, all the way to the very top, within the agencies involved in the processing of these chartered flights.)
"Hindi ako maniniwala na 'yung sarhento lamang ang involved. Meron pa," he added.
(I won't believe that only the sergeant is involved. There are other more.)

To recall, Interior and Local Government Secretary Jonvic Remulla identified the Mindanao politician allegedly involved in the attempted drug smuggling as former Bangsamoro Parliament member Edriezan Hadji Nasser Rimbang.
Remulla had said Rimbang allegedly paid Mendoza for the landing rights and the private hangar where the plane was supposed to land from Laos in the last week of September.
Philippine National Police (PNP) chief Police General Jose Melencio Nartatez Jr. said Mendoza has been relieved from her post and is now under restrictive custody at the Aviation Security Group.
Rimbang, meanwhile, denied involvement in the attempted drug smuggling. — VDV, GMA News
